meta.blurb: Leila forgot a colleague's name today, and her keys again. Her nephew Ravi, a neuroscience student, takes her on daily walks along the canal and explains what exercise may do for memory, focus and mood, and what it cannot do.
meta.bible: Leila: a fifty-five-year-old bookkeeper in a small town, kind and a little worried about her memory. Ravi: her nephew, twenty-six, a neuroscience student who stays with her for a month and explains the brain on daily walks along the Canal path. The town has a Canal, a Market square and a community hall with a dance class. Key terms: Neuron, Synapse, Hippocampus, Aerobic, BDNF, Cortisol, Endorphins, Dementia, Randomised trial, Moderate, Vigorous. The science is real and hedged: much of the work on BDNF and new brain cells comes from animals; studies in people are often small or mixed; exercise helps but is not a cure or a guarantee; no invented numbers or studies. Guideline used: adults are advised to aim for about one hundred and fifty to three hundred minutes of moderate activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening on two days (the World Health Organization advice). Cast and places added for the full book: Meena is Leila's older sister and Ravi's mother, who phones often. Marcus is the colleague whose name Leila forgot; he works at the next desk in the office on Market square. Mr Hughes is a retired postman and neighbour in his seventies who walks with a stick, swims twice a week and has a dog called Biscuit. Joan is Leila's friend, who has felt low since retiring. Nadia teaches the Thursday dance class at the community hall. Dr Amin is Leila's family doctor. The Lock Cafe stands beside the canal near Willow Bridge. Leila's mother had dementia in her seventies and died the winter before the story begins, which is why Leila worries and why her house feels quiet; a family history can raise the chance a little but is not a sentence. Ravi stays four weeks in autumn, and the story runs from one Friday to the Sunday after he leaves. Leila does not have a husband in the story and lives alone in a terraced house near the canal. More key terms: Seahorse, Dopamine, Serotonin, Endocannabinoids, Plasticity, Neurotransmitters, Cortex, Circadian, Sedentary, Resistance, Insulin, Inflammation, Myokines, Sarcopenia, Apnoea, Executive, Stroop, Tai Chi, Yoga, Mediterranean, Alzheimer's, Cognitive, Dehydration, Axon, Dendrites, Glucose, Oxygen, Capillaries, Neurogenesis, Vitamin, Melatonin, Physiotherapist. Facts used, all hedged in the text: about eighty-six billion neurons; the brain is about two percent of body weight and uses roughly a fifth of the body's energy; BDNF and new-neuron evidence is mostly from animals and adult neurogenesis is debated; a one-year walking trial in about one hundred and twenty older adults found the hippocampus grew by about two percent in the walkers, and later studies were mixed; London taxi drivers have a larger back part of the hippocampus; a Finnish trial called FINGER combined exercise, food, brain training and health checks; habits took about sixty-six days on average to form, with a very wide range; about one in three people over sixty-five fall each year; the ten-thousand-step target began as a Japanese pedometer slogan in the nineteen-sixties; a Lancet expert commission lists about fourteen risk factors for dementia and estimated that nearly half of cases might in theory be delayed or prevented, an uncertain estimate; most adults need about seven to nine hours of sleep. Voice: friendly, curious, honest about what is not known. Nobody gets personal medical advice. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

beats.scene: Leila searches her bag and coat pockets at her front door
beats.summary: Leila, a bookkeeper of fifty-five, comes home on a Friday evening and cannot find her keys.

beats.scene: A colleague waits politely at the next desk while Leila hesitates
beats.summary: At work that afternoon Leila could not remember the name of her colleague Marcus.

beats.scene: Leila holds up her keys, relieved, then sits down very still
beats.summary: She finds the keys in a zipped inside pocket and remembers her mother's dementia.

beats.scene: Leila on the telephone in her kitchen beside a wall calendar
beats.summary: Her sister Meena phones to ask whether Ravi can stay for a month.

beats.scene: Ravi stands at Leila's door with a rucksack, grinning
beats.summary: Ravi arrives on Saturday morning, a twenty-six-year-old neuroscience student, and hugs his aunt.

beats.scene: Leila and Ravi sit at a kitchen table with two cups of tea
beats.summary: Over tea Leila admits to the lost keys and the forgotten name, and Ravi listens calmly.

beats.scene: Ravi raises one hand like a promise beside an open notebook
beats.summary: Ravi says he is a student, not a doctor, and promises an honest account of the evidence.

beats.scene: Leila and Ravi shake hands over the kettle with a notebook between them
beats.summary: They agree a deal: a walk along the canal every morning and a notebook for questions.

beats.scene: Leila folds her arms, doubtful, while Ravi smiles beside the window
beats.summary: Leila doubts that she can start exercise at fifty-five; Ravi says that older people have improved too.

beats.scene: Bright trainers stand by the front door beside an old canvas bag
beats.summary: Ravi admits that he sits for hours too, so the walks are for them both, and Leila sets out her shoes.

beats.scene: A rough brain sketched on the back of an envelope, covered in dots
beats.summary: Over Sunday breakfast Ravi draws a brain on an envelope and says it has about eighty-six billion neurons.

beats.scene: A single branching nerve cell drawn large, with its parts labelled
beats.summary: A neuron has a body, branches called dendrites that listen, and a long axon that sends messages.

beats.scene: Two nerve cells with a tiny gap and glowing dots crossing it
beats.summary: At each synapse, a tiny gap between neurons, chemical messengers carry the signal across.

beats.scene: A bright pulse racing along a long thread between glowing cells
beats.summary: Every thought and movement is a pattern of electrical and chemical signals moving through the web.

beats.scene: Leila draws a filing cabinet and Ravi crosses it out beside a web
beats.summary: A memory is not kept in one drawer but is a pattern spread across many connections.

beats.scene: A grass field with a pale path being worn by many footsteps
beats.summary: Practice strengthens synapses, as walking wears a path across a field.

beats.scene: Leila smiles with relief as Ravi points to a diagram of new branches
beats.summary: This ability to change is called plasticity, and it lasts all through life, so older brains can learn.

beats.scene: Leila raises one finger, the word just out of reach
beats.summary: Forgetting is normal and even useful, and names are hard because they tell us nothing about a person.

beats.scene: A tired woman surrounded by words: late, stress, noise, hungry, worry
beats.summary: Tiredness, stress, poor sleep, low mood and doing too much at once all make forgetting more likely.

beats.scene: Leila sets a phone alarm beside a glass of water and her trainers
beats.summary: Ravi says the brain is not a muscle but responds to how we live; Leila sets her alarm.

beats.scene: A glowing brain beside a battery with one fifth lit up
beats.summary: Before the first walk Ravi says the brain is two percent of body weight but uses roughly a fifth of its energy.

beats.scene: Red blood vessels branch around a brain carrying small glowing drops
beats.summary: Blood delivers oxygen and glucose to the brain, which stores very little, so steady blood flow matters.

beats.scene: Leila and Ravi walk briskly along a misty canal at dawn, ducks nearby
beats.summary: On the first morning walk along the canal Leila's heart beats faster as she walks briskly.

beats.scene: Leila presses two fingers to her wrist while Ravi watches a clock
beats.summary: During exercise the heart and breathing speed up and more blood flows to the brain; they count Leila's pulse.

beats.scene: Three small drawings of a walker, a cyclist and a swimmer
beats.summary: Aerobic exercise is any steady activity that raises the heart rate for a while, such as walking, cycling or swimming.

beats.scene: A simple drawing of a heart, lungs and muscles glowing
beats.summary: In the body, breathing quickens and the heart pumps more blood; over weeks the heart grows stronger and the resting pulse slows.

beats.scene: A heart and a brain joined by red tubes in a simple drawing
beats.summary: What is good for the heart is generally good for the brain's small vessels; high blood pressure harms them and exercise can lower it a little.

beats.scene: Tiny red vessels branching through a mouse brain beside a running wheel
beats.summary: In animals exercise grows new small blood vessels in the brain; in people this is hard to see, so it is uncertain.

beats.scene: Leila sits on a cafe chair, flushed and smiling, with a glass of water
beats.summary: Leila is tired but pleased after the walk, and Ravi says to start at a pace she can keep up.

beats.scene: Leila hangs her keys on a hook by her front door, smiling
beats.summary: Back home Leila has lost nothing all morning, but Ravi says that one good morning is a story, not evidence.

beats.scene: A small glowing molecule shaped like a key beside a nerve cell
beats.summary: Ravi explains that exercise raises a protein called BDNF, which helps neurons survive, grow and connect.

beats.scene: A test tube of blood beside a walker and a small rising chart
beats.summary: In people, one session of exercise raises BDNF in the blood for a while, but blood levels are not brain levels.

beats.scene: A happy mouse runs on a wheel in a cage, whiskers blown back
beats.summary: Most of the evidence on BDNF comes from mice and rats running on wheels.

beats.scene: A mouse and a woman side by side with a question mark between them
beats.summary: Animals can be studied inside the brain, but mice are not people, so results must be checked in humans.

beats.scene: A young glowing neuron sprouting among older ones in an animal brain
beats.summary: In animals, exercise increases new brain cells in the hippocampus, a process called neurogenesis.

beats.scene: Two scientists argue over thin brain slices beside a microscope
beats.summary: Whether adult humans make many new neurons is debated: some studies find them and others find very few.

beats.scene: Ravi counts helpers on his fingers as they cross Willow Bridge
beats.summary: Exercise probably acts in many ways at once, and which matter most in people is not known.

beats.scene: Leila gazes at an old framed photograph of her mother on a mantelpiece
beats.summary: Leila voices her fear about her mother's illness; Ravi says a family history can raise the chance a little but is not a sentence.

beats.scene: A fragile bridge of planks between a mouse wheel and a walking woman
beats.summary: A good explanation of how something might work is not proof that it works; trials in people are needed.

beats.scene: Leila's open notebook with three questions, lit by a bedside lamp
beats.summary: Leila writes three questions in her notebook and Ravi adds the word hippocampus for tomorrow.

beats.scene: A seahorse-shaped part glowing inside a drawing of a head
beats.summary: The hippocampus, named for the Greek word for seahorse, lies deep in each side of the brain and is vital for memory.

beats.scene: A librarian files glowing cards while older memories wait on shelves behind
beats.summary: The hippocampus helps to form new memories of events, and damage to it makes new memories hard to form.

beats.scene: A black taxi on a London street beside a map crowded with tiny streets
beats.summary: London taxi drivers, who memorise thousands of streets, have a larger back part of the hippocampus.

beats.scene: A hippocampus shrinking slightly across a row of calendar years
beats.summary: The hippocampus tends to shrink slowly with age, so scientists ask whether exercise can slow the change.

beats.scene: Two groups of older adults, one walking on a track, one stretching
beats.summary: In a famous one-year trial of about one hundred and twenty older adults, the walkers' hippocampus grew by about two percent.

beats.scene: Ravi shakes his head at a graph that rises and then flattens
beats.summary: Later studies were more mixed, and a bigger hippocampus does not always mean a better memory.

beats.scene: Two similar parking spaces side by side, one marked yesterday and one today
beats.summary: The hippocampus also keeps similar memories apart, such as where the keys were put today and yesterday.

beats.scene: A student studies a list of pictures, then a clock and a jogger
beats.summary: In one small study, exercise four hours after learning helped memories last, but more research is needed.

beats.scene: Leila at the office with sticky notes of tiny sketches beside colleagues' desks
beats.summary: Leila learns her colleagues' names with vivid images, and Ravi says attention comes first.

beats.scene: Leila greets Marcus at his desk, smiling, a sticky note on his screen
beats.summary: Leila greets Marcus by name, admits she forgot it, and finds that honesty about forgetting lifts her mood.

beats.scene: Two groups drawn side by side, one walking briskly and one sitting
beats.summary: Studies often find that active people think better, but active people may differ in many other ways.

beats.scene: A person sits down slowly while a pale shadow of illness follows behind
beats.summary: Cause and effect can run backwards: a changing brain may make a person less active.

beats.scene: A coin flipping above two groups of volunteers being sorted by chance
beats.summary: A randomised trial assigns volunteers by chance, so the groups start alike.

beats.scene: One group walks while another group stretches on mats
beats.summary: The comparison group may stretch or carry on as usual, and nobody can be blind to exercise, so expectations may play a part.

beats.scene: Ravi holds a notebook with two columns of results and question marks
beats.summary: Randomised trials give a more mixed but still hopeful picture, with modest benefits for thinking in some adults.

beats.scene: A tall stack of review papers, one marked small, another marked none
beats.summary: Large reviews do not always agree: some find little benefit in healthy older adults and others find small gains.

beats.scene: A small step on a path beside a giant leap crossed out
beats.summary: Where trials find a benefit, it is usually modest: a helpful nudge, not a transformation.

beats.scene: A thick file of exciting results beside a thin pile of dull ones
beats.summary: Publication bias: exciting results are more likely to be published, so the record can look rosier than the truth.

beats.scene: Leila and Ravi on a bench, Leila holding up both palms, questioning
beats.summary: Exercise also helps the heart, bones, mood and sleep, and the risks are small for most people, so it is worth doing.

beats.scene: A notebook page headed Four Questions with four drawn question marks
beats.summary: Leila writes four questions to ask of any health claim: who, how many, compared with what, and how big.

beats.scene: Three small cards on a table: a chess piece, a clock and a juggler
beats.summary: Executive functions are planning, switching tasks and holding attention, where reviews often find the clearest effects of exercise.

beats.scene: Cards with colour words printed in clashing ink fan out on a table
beats.summary: Ravi tests Leila with the Stroop test, naming ink colours instead of reading the words.

beats.scene: The front of a brain glowing with tiny blood vessels and chemical dots
beats.summary: The front of the brain depends on blood flow and chemical signals that exercise changes, so it may respond well.

beats.scene: Leila at her door, a phone in one hand, keys in the other
beats.summary: Leila realises that the lost keys were a problem of attention: she zipped them away while on the phone.

beats.scene: Leila says her words aloud as she hangs her keys on a hook
beats.summary: Leila begins saying aloud keys on the hook, giving the memory a second of real attention.

beats.scene: A walker strides along a garden path while a clock shows ten minutes
beats.summary: One session of exercise can briefly improve attention afterwards, so a ten-minute walk before a hard task may help.

beats.scene: Schoolchildren spill into a playground while a teacher holds the door
beats.summary: Some studies find that children concentrate better in class after an active break.

beats.scene: Leila finishes a tall pile of files at her desk, trainers under it
beats.summary: Leila finishes her accounts early on Monday, but Ravi says one busy day proves nothing.

beats.scene: A juggler tosses many balls while one slips from his hands
beats.summary: Multitasking is largely a myth: the brain switches between tasks, and each switch costs time and accuracy.

beats.scene: Ravi frowns at a laptop while Leila holds out his coat
beats.summary: Ravi is stuck on his project, Leila sends him for a walk, and he returns with the answer.

beats.scene: Leila stretches her arms wide on a bright morning at the canal
beats.summary: After half an hour of brisk walking Leila feels lighter and calmer, and Ravi says that exercise can affect mood.

beats.scene: A smiling walker with small sparkles drawn around her head
beats.summary: Exercise may release endorphins, the body's own painkillers, and scans of runners show signs of this.

beats.scene: A crowded kitchen with many cooks stirring pots labelled with chemical names
beats.summary: Dopamine, serotonin and endocannabinoids may matter too, and scientists are still sorting out which count most.

beats.scene: Sunlight on water, rhythmic footsteps and a small tick mark
beats.summary: Fresh air, daylight, rhythm and a sense of achievement also lift the mood of a walk.

beats.scene: A cup of tea and a clock beside a calm figure walking away
beats.summary: Cortisol, the stress hormone, rises briefly during exercise and then settles; regular exercise may soften the stress response.

beats.scene: A hunter runs from a tiger while an office worker sits frozen
beats.summary: Stress prepares the body to fight or flee, but modern worries keep us sitting; a walk gives that energy somewhere to go.

beats.scene: Leila and Marcus walk round Market square at lunchtime with sandwiches
beats.summary: Under deadline stress Leila walks round Market square at lunch, and Marcus joins her and feels calmer too.

beats.scene: A walker counts breaths in time with her steps beside the canal
beats.summary: Ravi teaches slow breathing in time with steps, in for four steps and out for four, which can calm the body.

beats.scene: A tight knot loosening into a smooth ribbon above a walker
beats.summary: Exercise can reduce anxiety symptoms, but it is not a cure and severe anxiety needs a doctor.

beats.scene: A notebook page with a row of small faces and a rising line
beats.summary: Leila starts a mood diary, scoring her mood before and after each walk; Ravi says feelings are not proof but useful information.

beats.scene: A grey cloud above a bench with a sunny walking path beside it
beats.summary: Reviews find exercise can reduce symptoms of mild to moderate depression, but it is not a replacement for treatment.

beats.scene: Two faces, one smiling and one under a heavy grey cloud
beats.summary: Depression is more than sadness and can dull concentration, so a low person may think their memory is failing.

beats.scene: A walker leaving a house into daylight, leaving a swirling thought cloud behind
beats.summary: Exercise may lift a low mood by bringing daylight, company, better sleep and a break from brooding.

beats.scene: A calendar with two weeks circled beside a phone showing a doctor's number
beats.summary: If low mood lasts two weeks or more, talk to a doctor; help is available, and in a crisis contact an emergency service.

beats.scene: A person in socks at a door, one trainer in hand, a ten-minute timer
beats.summary: Exercise feels hardest when mood is low, so the trick is a tiny start, because action often comes before motivation.

beats.scene: Joan in a heavy coat stands with Leila on the canal path
beats.summary: Joan, low since retiring, visits, and Leila asks her only to walk to the corner and back.

beats.scene: Leila at the kitchen table with both hands round a mug
beats.summary: Leila admits that part of her worry is grief; after her mother died she slept badly and forgot much.

beats.scene: A thought bubble crowded with worries leaving little space for new facts
beats.summary: Worrying about forgetting uses up attention, so anxiety about memory can make forgetting worse.

beats.scene: A notebook page of mood scores with a gentle upward slant
beats.summary: Leila's mood diary shows higher scores after most walks; Ravi says her brain is not broken, only busy.

beats.scene: Rain on a window, a woman on a sofa, trainers unused by the door
beats.summary: On a flat rainy Sunday Leila skips her walk; Ravi says one bad day is not failure and suggests a ten-minute minimum walk.

beats.scene: A calm walker passes through trees with soft green light on the path
beats.summary: A walk among trees and grass may feel calming, though scientists are still working out why.

beats.scene: One walker beside a roaring road, another among trees, with small thought clouds
beats.summary: In a small study, people who walked ninety minutes in nature brooded less than people who walked beside a busy road.

beats.scene: Leaves, water and birds gently catching the eye of a relaxed walker
beats.summary: One theory says natural scenes hold attention gently and let the tired focusing system rest, but evidence is mixed.

beats.scene: The rising sun over the canal with a small eye drawn in the corner
beats.summary: Morning daylight helps set the body's internal clock, which affects sleep and alertness.

beats.scene: A sun beside a bone, and a pale winter sky
beats.summary: Sunlight lets the skin make vitamin D for bones and muscles; in northern winters many people make little, and a doctor can advise.

beats.scene: Golden leaves fall on the path as Leila wraps her scarf tighter
beats.summary: In autumn cold, Leila learns to walk in layers, since there is no bad weather, only the wrong clothes.

beats.scene: Ducks and a narrowboat on still water with a walker standing beside
beats.summary: Some studies link being near water with better wellbeing; the research is young.

beats.scene: A city street with a few trees, window boxes and a small park bench
beats.summary: Even a small park, a tree-lined street or window plants can give a little green; any green is better than none.

beats.scene: A busy road with traffic fumes beside a quiet lane
beats.summary: Air pollution is linked with a higher risk of dementia, so quiet streets and paths are a sensible choice where possible.

beats.scene: Leila stands still beside the water, watching a grey heron
beats.summary: Ravi asks Leila to stop and notice five things; she watches a heron, learning that quiet attention can be trained.

beats.scene: A bed and a moonlit window with running shoes at the door
beats.summary: After two weeks of walks Leila sleeps better, and Ravi says exercise tends to help sleep and sleep helps memory.

beats.scene: Glowing memories drift from a seahorse shape into a wide cloud of connections
beats.summary: In deep sleep the hippocampus replays the day's events and helps move them into longer-term storage, called consolidation.

beats.scene: A moonlit brain washed by a gentle blue tide
beats.summary: In mice, the brain may clear away waste more efficiently during sleep; whether this is as strong in people is not yet known.

beats.scene: A clock showing five hours beside a tired figure with a heavy head
beats.summary: Most adults need about seven to nine hours of sleep, and too little harms attention and memory.

beats.scene: A walker in daylight beside a sleeping figure under a smiling moon
beats.summary: Reviews find that regular exercise modestly improves sleep.

beats.scene: A runner at sunset beside a bedside lamp
beats.summary: Most people sleep fine after evening exercise, but a few are wired after hard effort near bedtime, so experiment.

beats.scene: A phone, a coffee cup and a wine glass beside a bed, crossed out
beats.summary: Caffeine lasts for hours, alcohol makes sleep lighter, bright screens delay sleep, and a dark cool room helps.

beats.scene: A short nap on a sofa with a small clock showing twenty minutes
beats.summary: A short nap of about twenty minutes may refresh, but long or late naps can disturb night sleep.

beats.scene: Ravi asleep on the sofa, snoring, a laptop on his chest
beats.summary: Loud snoring with pauses in breathing and heavy tiredness may be sleep apnoea, which a doctor can test.

beats.scene: A notebook sleep chart with small moons and a gentle rising line
beats.summary: Leila adds sleep to her diary and after a week gets nearly seven hours, having stopped answering emails at midnight.

beats.scene: An office worker sits still while a clock shows many hours passing
beats.summary: Leila finds she sits for almost eight hours a day, and long sitting is linked with poorer health.

beats.scene: A row of tall office chairs and one tiny walking figure far away
beats.summary: Sitting and exercising are separate habits: a morning walk helps but does not fully cancel a long day in a chair.

beats.scene: A kitchen timer on a desk while Leila rises from her chair
beats.summary: Leila sets a timer to ring every thirty minutes and walks to the window or makes tea each time.

beats.scene: A heart beside a bar showing blood sugar dipping smoothly after short walks
beats.summary: Small studies show that breaking up sitting with short light walks gives steadier blood sugar after meals.

beats.scene: A brain scan beside a chair and a calendar
beats.summary: In one small study, more sitting was linked with a thinner memory-related brain area, which shows a link but not a cause.

beats.scene: A standing desk beside a plain desk, a person shifting feet
beats.summary: Standing is slightly better than sitting but is not magic; the best plan is to change position and keep moving.

beats.scene: Leila walks beside Marcus round Market square with notebooks and coffee
beats.summary: Leila and Marcus try walking meetings; a small study found more creative ideas while walking.

beats.scene: A television screen showing an advert while a person marches on the spot
beats.summary: Leila stands and moves during television advert breaks; small bursts of light movement add up.

beats.scene: Ravi stretches his aching back beside an untidy desk of papers
beats.summary: Ravi admits his back aches from sitting, and they agree a shared rule: stand every half hour, walk every two hours.

beats.scene: A step counter on a wrist showing a number and a small upward arrow
beats.summary: Leila borrows Ravi's step counter and finds she takes about three thousand steps on an office day, then decides to add a little each week.

beats.scene: A poster showing a clock and a weekly calendar with walking figures
beats.summary: Health guidelines advise adults to aim for about 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week.

beats.scene: A short bar of hard minutes equal to a longer bar of gentle minutes
beats.summary: Seventy-five to 150 minutes of vigorous activity can meet the same target, with vigorous minutes counting about double.

beats.scene: Two friends walking and chatting without struggling for breath
beats.summary: The talk test: at a moderate pace you can talk but not sing; at a vigorous pace you can say only a few words.

beats.scene: A calendar with short ten-minute bars adding up to thirty
beats.summary: Activity can be collected in short bouts, and any length counts towards the weekly total.

beats.scene: A pedometer showing ten thousand beside an old Japanese shop sign
beats.summary: The ten-thousand-step target began as a Japanese pedometer slogan in the 1960s; benefits seem to level off at six to eight thousand for older adults.

beats.scene: A staircase where the first steps are tall and the later steps small
beats.summary: The biggest gains come when the least active begin to move a little, so anything is better than nothing.

beats.scene: A scale from zero to ten with a walker marked at six
beats.summary: A zero to ten effort scale: moderate is about five or six and vigorous about seven or eight.

beats.scene: A tired runner beside a bed, a rest day circled on a calendar
beats.summary: More is not always better: the effects level off, and rest days let the body recover.

beats.scene: A weekly timetable with short walks on seven days
beats.summary: Leila totals her week of morning walks and lunchtime laps at well over two hundred minutes.

beats.scene: Plain shoes beside a dusty gym membership card in a drawer
beats.summary: Leila decides she does not need a gym; shoes and a path are enough, though a gym helps those who like it.

beats.scene: Leila lifts two full water bottles beside a kitchen table
beats.summary: Ravi says strength training matters too, and shows Leila how to use water bottles as weights.

beats.scene: A tall shadow of muscle shrinking slowly beside a long calendar
beats.summary: From midlife the body slowly loses muscle unless it is used, which is called sarcopenia, and strength matters for daily life.

beats.scene: A glowing arm muscle sends small messengers along a vessel towards a brain
beats.summary: Working muscles release chemical messengers called myokines, and scientists are studying whether some reach the brain.

beats.scene: Two chart lines, one for older adults lifting weights and one for stretching
beats.summary: Some trials suggest resistance training modestly improves thinking in older adults, but the evidence is still developing.

beats.scene: Leila lowers herself to a kitchen chair, arms out, while Ravi counts
beats.summary: Work all the major muscle groups on two or more days a week with simple exercises such as chair stands and bottle lifts.

beats.scene: Leila rises from a chair and wobbles, laughing, as Ravi offers a hand
beats.summary: Leila wobbles on her first chair stands and laughs; Ravi says a little struggle is the point.

beats.scene: Leila lifts a bottle slowly with steady breath and careful posture
beats.summary: Safety rules for strength work: move slowly, breathe out on effort, start light, stop at sharp pain, ask a doctor with health problems.

beats.scene: Leila swaps a water bottle for a bag of rice, adding weight gradually
beats.summary: Muscles grow when asked for a little more, so Leila swaps bottles for bags of rice and adds repetitions.

beats.scene: A strong bone beside a weak bone, and a woman stepping firmly
beats.summary: Strength and impact work help keep bones strong, which matters after the menopause, and a doctor can advise.

beats.scene: Leila carries two heavy shopping bags up her front steps, smiling
beats.summary: After weeks of strength work Leila carries shopping easily, and Ravi says everyday function is what strength is for.

beats.scene: Leila and a group of neighbours learn a dance step in a hall
beats.summary: Leila joins Nadia's Thursday dance class at the community hall, where neighbours learn one simple step.

beats.scene: Dancers move in a line while music notes and speech bubbles float above
beats.summary: Dance combines aerobic effort, rhythm, memory for steps, music and company in one activity.

beats.scene: A person learning to juggle with a faint brain scan glowing beside
beats.summary: In a small study, learning to juggle over three months grew some brain areas, which shrank again when practice stopped.

beats.scene: Two small groups, one dancing in a hall and one on exercise bikes
beats.summary: A small German study found that dance and fitness training both grew parts of the hippocampus, but only dance clearly improved balance.

beats.scene: Leila trips over a step, laughing, while Nadia claps the beat
beats.summary: Leila stumbles over a new step, and mistakes are part of learning because effortful learning goes deeper.

beats.scene: Headphones, a music note and a walker with a bouncing step
beats.summary: Music makes exercise feel easier and helps keep a steady pace, and Ravi makes Leila a walking playlist.

beats.scene: A crossword beside a language book and a set of paints
beats.summary: Brain games are less proven than people think; learning a real new skill keeps the mind more active.

beats.scene: Leila at a library table with a beginner's Spanish book and a pencil

B1B2: Leila reaches her front door on Friday evening and cannot find her keys. She turns out her bag, then each pocket of her coat, and her fingers find only tissues and receipts.
That afternoon, Leila wanted to introduce a client to Marcus, who has sat at the next desk for six years. His name vanished completely, and it only came back on the bus ride home.
At last she finds the keys, zipped into an inside pocket that she never uses. She laughs, but not for long, because she remembers her mother, who lost her memory in her seventies.
That evening her sister Meena phones to say that Ravi needs a quiet place to write his university project. Leila says yes at once, because she has not had a visitor in the house for a long time.
Ravi arrives on Saturday morning with a rucksack on his back and a cheerful smile. He is twenty-six, he studies the brain at university, and he hugs his aunt as if he has not seen her for years.
Over tea that evening, Leila tells Ravi about the lost keys and the forgotten name. He listens carefully and does not laugh, and he does not look worried either.
Ravi says that he is a student and not a doctor, so he cannot say what is wrong with anyone. He can tell her what researchers know, though, and he thinks that moving the body may help the mind.
They agree on a simple deal that will last for the whole month. Every morning they will walk beside the canal, and Leila will write her questions in a notebook.
Leila says that fifty-five is too old to begin, and that she has never liked sport. Ravi answers that studies have included people in their seventies and eighties, and many of them improved.
Ravi admits that he spends hours at a desk himself, so the walks will be good for both of them. Before she goes to bed, Leila finds her old trainers and sets them by the door.
On Sunday morning, Ravi draws a brain on the back of an envelope. He says it holds about eighty-six billion nerve cells, which are called neurons.
Ravi draws a neuron with a round body, many short branches and one long thread. The branches listen for messages from other cells, and the long thread sends messages onward.
The gap between two neurons is called a synapse, and it is far too small to see. A signal reaches the end of one cell, and tiny chemical messengers carry it across to the next.

Inside each neuron the signal is a tiny electrical pulse, and between neurons it is chemical. Every thought, memory or movement is a pattern of these signals, and it all happens in thousandths of a second.

Leila imagines memories sitting in drawers, like the files in her office. Ravi shakes his head and says that a memory is a pattern spread across many connections, more like a web than a filing cabinet.
Ravi compares learning to walking across a field of long grass. The first walk leaves no mark, but after many walks a path appears, and practice strengthens a connection in the same way.
The word for this is plasticity, which means that the brain can change its own connections. It does this at every age, so older brains can still learn new things, and Leila feels relieved.

Ravi says that forgetting is normal, and even useful, because the brain cannot keep every detail. Names are especially hard, because a name tells you nothing about the person, so almost everyone has one on the tip of the tongue.

Ravi lists other things that make us forget: tiredness, stress, poor sleep, low mood and trying to do too many things at once. Leila realises that she has worked late every night since the tax returns began to pile up.
Ravi says that the brain is not a muscle, but it does respond to the way we live. Leila writes her first question in the notebook, sets her alarm for seven, and goes to bed early.
Before the first walk, Ravi tells Leila that the brain weighs only about two percent of the body. It uses roughly a fifth of the body's energy, though, so it is a very hungry organ.
The brain gets its oxygen and sugar from the blood, and it can store very little of either. That means a steady flow of blood matters a great deal, every minute of the day.
On Monday morning they set off along the canal path, past ducks and a moored narrowboat. Leila walks briskly, and soon she can feel her heart beating faster.
They stop on a bench, and Ravi shows Leila how to find her pulse on her wrist. She counts it for fifteen seconds, and the number is much higher than it was at breakfast.
Ravi says that aerobic exercise is any steady activity that raises the heart rate for a while. Walking, cycling, swimming and dancing all count, and the word comes from the Greek word for air.
When Leila walks, her breathing quickens and her heart pumps more blood to her muscles. If she keeps walking for weeks, her heart will grow stronger and her pulse at rest may slow down.

What is good for the heart is generally good for the small blood vessels of the brain. High blood pressure can damage those vessels over the years, and regular exercise lowers blood pressure a little.
Studies in mice show that running can grow new tiny blood vessels in some parts of the brain. Nobody can look so closely inside a living human brain, so the same effect is still uncertain in people.
Back at the Lock Cafe, Leila sits down with a glass of water and a flushed face. She is tired but pleased, and Ravi tells her that it is wise to start at a pace she can keep up.
Back at home, Leila notices that she has not lost anything all morning. Ravi smiles, but he says that one good morning is a story and not evidence.
On Tuesday morning, Ravi says that exercise raises a protein called BDNF. The protein helps nerve cells to survive, grow and connect, so some people call it fertiliser for the brain.
In studies of people, a session of exercise raises the level of BDNF in the blood for a while. However, blood is not the brain, so scientists cannot be sure what the number means.

Much of the evidence comes from mice and rats that run on little wheels in their cages. Leila jokes that she should buy a wheel, and Ravi says that the mice choose to run, which is useful for scientists.

Scientists study animals because they can look inside the brain in ways that are not allowed with people. However, a mouse is not a person, and results must be checked in humans before anyone trusts them.

In mice, running increases the number of new brain cells in a part called the hippocampus. Scientists call the birth of new neurons neurogenesis, and Ravi says that the idea is much easier to state than to prove in people.

In people, some studies have found new neurons in adult brains, while others have found very few. Scientists are still arguing about it, and Ravi says that an honest scientist must say "we do not know yet."

Ravi counts on his fingers the other ways that exercise might help the brain. It may improve blood flow, calm inflammation, control blood sugar and raise growth factors, but scientists do not know which matter most in people.

Leila looks at the photograph of her mother and says what she is most afraid of. Ravi says that a family history can raise the chance a little, but many people in that position never develop dementia.
Ravi says that a story about how something might work is not proof that it does work. Only careful tests on people can show whether walking really helps memory.

Before bed, Leila writes three questions in her notebook: what helps, how much is enough, and what counts as proof. Ravi adds a word underneath, hippocampus, and says that it will be tomorrow's subject.

On Wednesday Ravi shows Leila a drawing of the hippocampus, which looks like a small curled seahorse. There are two of them, one on each side of the brain, and they lie deep inside behind the temples.
The hippocampus is like a busy librarian who files the events of today so that they can be found later. When it is damaged, a person can find it very hard to make new memories.
Ravi tells her about taxi drivers in London, who must memorise thousands of streets. Scans showed that the back part of their hippocampus was larger than in other people.
The hippocampus tends to shrink slowly as people grow older, and it shrinks faster in dementia. Scientists wonder whether regular exercise can slow that change, and they have tested the question.

In a well-known trial, about one hundred and twenty older adults either walked or did stretching for a year. In the walkers, the hippocampus grew by about two percent, while in the stretching group it shrank a little.
Later studies have given more mixed results, and some have found no change at all. Besides, a bigger hippocampus does not always mean a better memory, so the story is hopeful but not finished.

Ravi says the hippocampus also keeps similar memories apart, such as where you put your keys today and where you put them yesterday. When that sorting is hard, a habit like using one hook can make life much easier.

Ravi describes a small study in which people learned pictures and then exercised either straight away or four hours later. The later group remembered more two days afterwards, but scientists need more research before they trust it.

Leila decides to use a memory trick at work, and gives each colleague's name a funny image. Ravi points out that attention comes first, because nobody can remember a name that they never really heard.
On Friday, Leila greets Marcus by name and tells him that she forgot it a week ago. He laughs and says that he forgets names all the time, and he feels glad that she mentioned it.

On Saturday, Ravi explains that many studies find that active people have better memory and thinking. However, active people may also eat better, earn more and have healthier hearts, so the exercise might not be the reason.

There is a second problem, which is that cause and effect can run in the opposite direction. A person whose brain has begun to change may become less active, so poor thinking might lead to inactivity, not the other way round.
The fairest test is a randomised trial, in which chance decides who exercises and who does not. Because the groups start out alike, any difference at the end is more likely to come from the exercise.
The other group, called the control group, may stretch or simply carry on as usual. Nobody can hide from a volunteer whether they are exercising, so hopes and expectations may play a part.
When Ravi looks at the trials, the picture is more mixed than the surveys, but it is still hopeful. Some trials find small gains in thinking, while others find little or no difference.

Some large reviews of many trials have found little clear benefit in healthy older adults. Others have found small gains, because they included different kinds of exercise, different tests and different people.
Where trials do find a benefit, it is usually modest, a small step and not a giant leap. Ravi says that exercise is a helpful nudge for the brain, not a transformation.

Ravi warns her about another problem, which is that exciting results are more likely to be published than dull ones. As a result, the published studies can make a treatment look better than it really is.
Leila asks whether all this walking is worth it if the brain benefit is only modest. Ravi says that exercise also helps the heart, bones, mood and sleep, and that the risks are small for most people.
Leila writes four questions at the top of a page: who took part, how many, compared with what, and how big was the effect? She decides to use them on the next health story that she reads.

Ravi lays out cards with colour words printed in the wrong colours, such as the word red in blue ink. Leila must say the colour of the ink, not the word, and she finds it surprisingly hard.

The front of the brain does the planning and focusing, and it depends on good blood flow. Exercise changes blood flow and several chemical signals, so this part of the brain may respond especially well.
Leila thinks back to the evening when she zipped her keys into the wrong pocket. She was on the phone to a client at the time, so her attention was elsewhere and the keys were never recorded.

The walk passes a primary school, and children rush out to play. Ravi says that some studies have found that children concentrate better in class after an active break.
On Monday, Leila finishes a big pile of accounts earlier than usual after her morning walk. She feels proud, but Ravi reminds her that a single busy day proves nothing.
Ravi explains that the brain does not really do two things at once. It switches quickly between them, and every switch costs a little time and attention, so single tasks are easier to remember.
That evening Ravi is stuck on a difficult paragraph of his project. Leila hands him his coat and says "Walk," and twenty minutes later he comes back with the answer.
On Tuesday, after half an hour of brisk walking, Leila stretches her arms wide at the canal. She feels lighter and calmer than she has felt for weeks, and she asks Ravi why.

Chemistry is only part of the story, because feelings do not come only from molecules. Fresh air, sunlight, steady rhythm and a sense of achievement can all lift the mood of a walk.

Cortisol is a stress hormone, and it rises for a short time during a workout and then settles. Over weeks, regular exercise may make the body's stress response less sharp, though scientists are still studying this.
Stress hormones prepare the body to fight or run away, but modern worries usually make us sit still at a desk. A walk gives that energy somewhere to go, and many people find that it settles them.
Leila has a deadline on Wednesday, so at lunchtime she walks round Market square instead of eating at her desk. Marcus joins her, and he says that he feels calmer and much less hungry for biscuits.

After a few weeks of strength exercises, Leila carries two heavy shopping bags up her front steps without puffing. Ravi says that being able to do everyday things is exactly what strength is for.

Ravi whispers that dancing is a clever kind of exercise, because it uses many skills at the same time. It raises the heart rate, and it asks the brain to remember steps, follow the beat and watch other people.

A small German study followed older adults for eighteen months, some dancing and some doing fitness training. Both groups showed growth in parts of the hippocampus, but the dancers improved their balance more.

Leila signs up for a beginners' Spanish class at the library on Tuesday evenings. She is nervous about learning words at her age, but she loves the first lesson and writes five new words in the notebook.

Ravi times Leila as she stands on one leg beside the kitchen counter. She holds the left leg for a long time, but the right leg lasts only a few seconds.

Leila meets Mr Hughes at the canal, and he tells her that he swims twice a week. The water holds his weight and is kind to his sore knees, so swimming and water exercise suit many people with joint pain.

Studies find that dog owners tend to walk more than people without dogs. Mr Hughes says that Biscuit is his personal trainer, who never takes a day off and never accepts excuses.
At the Lock Cafe, Leila mixes up two names and puts her hand over her mouth. Nobody minds, and Ravi says that being ashamed of forgetting can do more harm than forgetting itself.
Large studies and reviews link regular physical activity with a lower risk of dementia, in some reviews by roughly a quarter. This is a link, not a guarantee, and many other things matter too.

Ravi says that hearing loss in midlife is one of the largest risk factors on the list, and hearing aids may help. He also points out that a name that you did not hear properly can never be remembered.
High blood pressure and raised cholesterol in midlife both appear on the list of risk factors. They rarely cause symptoms, so a regular check with a nurse or doctor is the only way to know.

Ravi says that there is no single brain food. A Mediterranean-style diet, rich in vegetables, beans, nuts, fish and olive oil, is linked with better brain health, though the evidence is mostly observational.

Smoking harms the heart and the small blood vessels of the brain. Mr Hughes tells Leila that he stopped smoking forty years ago, and Ravi says that stopping helps at any age.

A trial in Finland, called FINGER, gave older adults at risk a mixture of exercise, healthy food, brain training and health checks. After two years they scored a little higher on thinking tests than a comparison group, although the difference was modest.

Ravi says that some changes are worth discussing with a doctor, such as repeating the same questions or getting lost on a familiar route. Many causes of memory trouble can be treated, so it is wise to ask early.
Leila finally visits Dr Amin and describes the lost keys, the forgotten name and her new routine. The doctor checks her blood pressure, asks careful questions and arranges some routine blood tests.

Leila decides to use the stairs at the office instead of the lift. Ravi says that short bursts of movement count, and that even ten minutes is better than none.

Some small studies suggest that very short, hard bursts of effort raise BDNF more than steady exercise. Ravi says that moderate activity is enough for most people, and that anyone with health worries should ask a doctor before trying hard bursts.

Ravi explains that habits form when a new action is linked to something that you already do every day. In one study, new habits took about two months on average to form, although the range was very wide.
Leila catches a bad cold and misses a whole week of walking, and she feels low about it. Ravi tells her to rest while she is ill, to return gently, and not to give up.
Ravi says that people keep up exercise that they enjoy, so enjoyment is not a luxury but a method. Leila decides to do more dancing and walking, and to leave out anything that she dreads.
Ravi explains that a vague goal such as getting fit is weaker than a clear plan. Leila writes a note for the fridge: after breakfast on weekdays, I will walk for twenty minutes.
Ravi gives Leila a list of safety habits for people who walk outdoors. Wear comfortable shoes with good grip, wear something bright in poor light, carry a phone and tell someone where you are going.
Leila hangs a calendar in the kitchen and ticks every day that she walks. After a good fortnight she rewards herself with a pair of thick new walking socks.
After four weeks, Leila has not lost her keys once, and she remembers her whole shopping list without writing it down. Ravi smiles, but he reminds her that many things could explain the change.
Leila asks Ravi whether her own month proves that exercise works. He says that she is one person with no comparison group, so her story is real and valuable, but it cannot prove anything.
Over their last walk but one, Ravi sums up the lesson once more. Exercise is not a magic pill, its effects on thinking are modest, and sleep, learning, food and friends all matter as well.

On a sheet of paper, Ravi makes three columns: well established, promising and unknown. Heart, mood, sleep and strength are in the first column, some thinking benefits are in the second, and the exact reasons are in the third.
Joan, Marcus, Mr Hughes and Nadia decide to start a regular Wednesday walk along the canal. They call themselves the Canal Walkers, and Biscuit leads the way.
At the end of the month, Ravi packs his rucksack and Leila walks with him to the station. She promises to keep walking, strengthening, dancing and writing in her notebook, and he promises to phone.
Back at home, Leila writes a plan for each week and sticks it on the fridge. It has brisk walks, strength exercises on two days, dance on Thursday, early nights and time with friends.
Dr Amin phones to say that the blood tests show nothing unusual. She suggests a review in six months, and she tells Leila to come sooner if her worries change.

On the first morning without Ravi, Leila walks alone in the drizzle, and she can almost hear his voice in her head. Back home, she finds her keys on the hook, and she writes in her notebook: start where you are.

On Sunday, Ravi calls, and Leila tells him that she has just finished a long walk beside the canal. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please ask a doctor about your own health.

In the office on Market square that afternoon, Leila had turned to introduce a visiting client to the man who had sat at the next desk for six years, and his name had vanished. She smiled, waved a hand in the air and said something vague, while Marcus waited with polite patience. The word came back only on the bus home, arriving all at once and bringing a hot wave of shame with it.

At last her fingers closed on the keys, zipped into an inside pocket that she had not touched in months. She laughed aloud on the doorstep, but the laugh faded quickly, because she was thinking of her mother. Her mother had developed dementia in her seventies, and Leila had watched that slow loss with a love and a helplessness she had never forgotten.

Her sister Meena telephoned that evening, as she often did, to ask whether Ravi could stay for a month while he completed a demanding research project. Leila agreed before the question was finished, because her house had felt strangely hollow ever since the winter. She mentioned neither the keys nor the forgotten name, and Meena, who knew her far too well, was not entirely convinced that all was well.

The next morning Ravi arrived on the doorstep with a heavy rucksack on his back and a grin that made him look about fifteen. He was twenty-six, a student of neuroscience with ink on his fingers and a month of work ahead of him, and he hugged his aunt so warmly that she forgot, for a moment, to be worried. Leila took his bag, showed him the small back bedroom and felt the whole house wake up around her.

Over tea that evening she told him everything: the keys, the vanished name and the fear that had been following her around for weeks. Ravi listened without once interrupting, and he did not laugh and he did not frown, which she found oddly comforting. When she had finished, he said that such slips are among the most common complaints in the world, and that they deserved a proper answer rather than a pat on the hand.

He was careful to say that he was a student and not a doctor, and that he could not tell her what, if anything, was wrong with her. What he could offer was an honest account of the research, including its gaps, because he believed that moving the body might well help the mind. He would tell her which findings were solid, which were hopeful, and which were no more than educated guesses.

Before bed they shook hands on a deal that would last for the whole of his stay. Every morning they would walk along the canal path, however the weather behaved, and while they walked Ravi would explain one piece of the puzzle. Leila, who trusted nothing that she had not written down, took a small blue notebook from the drawer of spare stationery and wrote the word Questions on the first page.

Leila confessed that she had never enjoyed sport, even at school, and that fifty-five seemed a ridiculous age to begin. Ravi answered that researchers had tested exercise on people in their seventies and eighties, and that fitness had improved in many of them, even when they started from almost nothing. Nobody, he said, could promise what it would do for any single person, but nobody was too old to try something gentle.

Ravi admitted, with a sheepish smile, that his own days were spent bent over a laptop, so the walks would do him as much good as they did her. Before she went to bed, Leila dug out a pair of trainers that she had bought years ago and never worn, and set them side by side at the foot of the stairs. They looked, she thought, like two small promises, and for the first time in weeks she fell asleep without listing everything she had forgotten.

On Sunday morning, over toast and a second pot of tea, Ravi drew a lopsided brain on the back of an envelope and covered it with dots. The human brain, he told her, contains roughly eighty-six billion nerve cells called neurons, which is more than ten times the number of people alive on Earth. Leila stared at the dots and tried, and failed, to imagine a crowd that large.

He drew a single neuron in close-up, with a round body, a bush of short branches called dendrites, and one long fibre called an axon that stretched across the envelope. The branches listen for incoming messages, he said, while the axon carries the cell's own message away towards its neighbours. Leila, who thought in columns of figures, found that a cell with an input and an output was almost comfortably familiar.

Where two neurons meet, Ravi explained, there is no real touching, only a gap so narrow that thousands of them would fit across the width of a hair. When a signal reaches the end of the axon, the cell releases chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, which drift across the gap and nudge the next cell into action. It was, he said, a little like passing a note along a row of children in a classroom, except that the note is a molecule and the classroom holds billions.

Inside a neuron, Ravi said, the signal travels as a tiny electrical pulse, and at each synapse it changes into a chemical one and then back again. Every thought, memory or movement is a pattern of such signals racing through the web, and the fastest of them cover many metres in a single second. Leila looked at her cup of tea and realised that choosing to lift it had involved more messages than she could ever count.

Leila, who spent her days among ledgers and filing cabinets, assumed that a memory must sit in a certain drawer, waiting to be pulled out. Ravi shook his head and explained that a memory is a pattern of connections spread across many regions, so that smell, sound, place and feeling are linked together like threads in a net. That is why one small cue, such as a song from childhood, can bring a whole afternoon flooding back, and why a name can be stubbornly hard to find when the threads around it are weak.

Learning, Ravi said, is like crossing a meadow of long grass: the first walker leaves hardly a trace, but after a hundred walkers a bare path appears. In the same way, every time we repeat a skill or revisit a fact, the synapses involved are used again and become stronger and more efficient, so that the signal passes more easily the next time. Forget it for long enough, he added, and the grass slowly grows back, which is why memories need to be visited.

Scientists call this ability plasticity, and Ravi said that it never switches off entirely, so that an older brain can still form new connections and learn new skills. It is slower than it was in childhood, and it needs effort and repetition, but it is real. Leila felt something loosen in her chest, because she had half believed that her brain was a finished building that could only decay.

Forgetting, Ravi said, is not a fault in the machine but part of its design, because a brain that kept every detail of every day would drown in trivia. Names are the hardest of all, since a name gives no clue about the person who carries it, and so it hangs by a single thread. Almost everyone has a word on the tip of the tongue at some time, he said, and that moment of being nearly able to say it is perfectly normal.

There are many other reasons for slips of memory, Ravi went on: tiredness, stress, poor sleep, low mood, hearing trouble, some medicines, and above all trying to do several things at the same time. Leila thought of the past two months, when the tax returns had piled up on her desk and she had eaten lunch standing, answered emails with the telephone on her shoulder and slept about five hours a night. "So perhaps I am not losing my mind," she said, "perhaps I am just losing my sleep."

Ravi was careful to add that the brain is not a muscle and does not grow stronger with every press-up, yet it responds to the way we live. Movement, he said, seems to be one of the signals it listens to, and Leila wrote her first real question in the notebook, which was how a walk could possibly reach as far as a neuron. She underlined it twice, set her alarm for seven o'clock, put a glass of water beside her trainers and went to bed before ten.

On Monday morning, while the porridge cooled, Ravi told her that the brain makes up only about two percent of the body's weight but burns roughly a fifth of its energy. It is the greediest organ she owned, he said, and it never stops working, even while she sleeps. Leila looked at the small bowl in front of her and felt, for the first time, a certain respect for her own head.

All that energy arrives in the blood, Ravi said, in the form of oxygen and a sugar called glucose, and the brain can store very little of either. It depends on a constant delivery through a network of vessels so fine that some of them are narrower than a hair. A few minutes without a good supply is enough to harm brain cells, which is why the health of those tiny pipes matters so much.

At seven o'clock on Monday the canal path was wrapped in a thin white mist, and the only company was a pair of ducks and a narrowboat with a curl of smoke rising from its chimney. Leila walked briskly, determined not to disgrace herself, and within a few minutes she could feel her heart thumping and her cheeks growing warm. "This is the easy part," said Ravi cheerfully, "so keep talking and keep walking."

They paused on a bench beside the old lock, and Ravi showed her how to press two fingers to her wrist and count the beats against his watch. Her pulse was much faster than it had been at breakfast, and he explained that during moderate exercise the heart pumps harder and more blood flows to the brain, along with everything else. This may be part of why people often feel clearer after a walk, he said, although the research on that is still unfolding.

Aerobic exercise, Ravi explained, is any steady activity that keeps the heart rate raised for a while, and the word comes from the Greek for air, because the muscles burn their fuel with the help of oxygen. Brisk walking qualifies, and so do cycling, swimming and dancing, as long as the effort is steady and the breathing is deeper than usual. Most of the research on exercise and the brain, he added, has tested this kind of activity.

During exercise the lungs take in more air, the heart pumps more blood with each beat, and the muscles collect the oxygen they need to keep going. If this is repeated week after week, Ravi said, the heart becomes a stronger pump, so that it needs fewer beats to do the same work and the pulse at rest often slows. Leila was pleased to learn that fitness was not a mysterious gift that some people were born with, but a change that anyone's body would make if asked politely and often.

The heart and the brain are closely linked, Ravi said, and what is good for one is generally good for the other, because the tiny vessels of the brain are as vulnerable as those that serve the heart. Years of high blood pressure can damage them, and regular exercise can lower blood pressure a little, although anyone with a blood pressure problem should speak to a doctor rather than rely on walking alone. That, he said, is one of the most solid reasons to believe that exercise helps the brain, and it has nothing to do with magic.

In mice, Ravi said, running can encourage the growth of new blood vessels in certain parts of the brain, which would give the neurons there a richer supply of oxygen. Nobody can examine the capillaries of a living human brain so closely, so whether the same thing happens in people, and how much, is still an open question. He seemed pleased to say so, and Leila realised that he enjoyed the edge of what is known more than the safe middle of it.

The walk ended at the Lock Cafe beside Willow Bridge, where Leila dropped onto a chair with a glass of water and cheeks the colour of tomatoes. Her calves ached and her lungs felt well used, yet she was smiling, and she was amazed to discover that she wanted to do it again tomorrow. Ravi told her that the best pace for a beginner is one that she can keep up, because an exercise plan that is abandoned after a week does nobody any good.

Back at home, Leila hung her keys on a hook by the door and realised, with a small shock of pleasure, that she had not lost a single thing all morning. She said so to Ravi, who smiled but shook his head, because he wanted her to understand a rule that scientists live by. One good morning is a story, he told her, and a story is not the same as evidence, which is exactly why he would spend the rest of the month teaching her the difference.

On Tuesday, as they walked beside a hedge with a few last blackberries, Ravi introduced her to a protein with an unwieldy name, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which everyone abbreviates to BDNF. It helps neurons to survive, to grow branches and to form connections, and some researchers describe it, loosely, as a kind of fertiliser for the brain. Exercise, he said, appears to raise its levels, but he asked her not to take the metaphor too literally.

Studies of volunteers have shown that BDNF rises in the blood after a session of exercise, and in some studies the rise is larger after harder effort. Yet blood is not brain, Ravi cautioned, and nobody is certain how closely the level in a blood sample reflects what is happening among the neurons. It was a pattern he would meet again and again in his field, a promising signal that was easy to measure and much harder to interpret.

Most of the evidence on BDNF, Ravi admitted, comes from mice and rats that were given a running wheel in their cages. Leila asked, with a perfectly straight face, whether she ought to buy one for her kitchen, and Ravi laughed so hard that a passing cyclist rang his bell at them. Mice actually love the wheels, he said, and run kilometres a night by choice, which makes them excellent volunteers for science.

Animal experiments allow researchers to do things that would never be permitted with people, such as examining brain tissue under a microscope after a period of running. The price of that freedom, Ravi said, is that a mouse brain differs from a human one in countless ways, and a result that holds for rodents has to be confirmed in humans before anyone can rely on it. "Mice are not small people," he said, and this was a sentence that Leila copied into her notebook.

One of the most striking results in animals, Ravi said, is that running increases the number of new neurons born in a part of the brain called the hippocampus, a region they would meet properly tomorrow. Scientists call this process neurogenesis, and it was once thought impossible in adults, because the old textbooks insisted that we are born with all the brain cells we will ever have. In mice the evidence is strong, but in people the picture is far murkier, and Ravi promised to explain exactly why.

In human brains the evidence is disputed: some careful studies have found signs of new neurons in adults well into old age, while others have found very few after childhood, and the two camps have argued for years. Ravi said that the methods used to examine brain tissue after death are difficult, and that reasonable experts read the same data in opposite ways. That, he told her gently, is the honest answer, and he said it would be wrong to pretend otherwise just because the story of new brain cells is so appealing.

BDNF was only one member of a large team, Ravi said, counting on his fingers as they crossed Willow Bridge. Exercise may also improve blood flow, calm the low-level inflammation that builds up in the body, help muscles to use blood sugar more effectively and raise other growth factors, any of which could matter for the brain. Which of them matter most in people, and in what order, is something that he and thousands of other researchers were still trying to work out.

That evening Leila looked for a long time at the photograph of her mother on the mantelpiece, and then finally said aloud what she was most afraid of. Ravi answered gently that a family history can raise the chance of dementia a little, but that it is not a sentence, and that many people with a parent who was affected never develop it themselves. What a person does with the years in between, he said, still seems to matter, and that was reason enough to keep walking.

A beautiful explanation of how something might work, Ravi said, is not the same as proof that it does work, and the history of medicine is full of ideas that sounded wonderful and failed in the clinic. Only careful tests on people, with fair comparisons and enough volunteers, can show whether walking truly improves memory, and those tests were exactly what they would discuss soon. Leila, who had spent thirty years checking that figures matched evidence, found that she agreed with every word.

Before bed, Leila turned to a fresh page of the blue notebook and wrote three questions in her neat bookkeeper's hand: what actually helps, how much is enough, and what counts as proof. Ravi read them over her shoulder with obvious approval, then added one word underneath in large capitals, which was HIPPOCAMPUS. Tomorrow, he promised, she would meet the part of her own head that was most closely linked with memory, and it was shaped like a seahorse.

On Wednesday, with a light rain freckling the canal, Ravi took out a drawing of the hippocampus, which gets its name from the Greek word for seahorse because of its curled, tapering shape. There are two of them, one tucked deep into each side of the brain behind the temples, each roughly as long as a finger. Leila put a hand to her head and tried, without success, to imagine a tiny seahorse swimming inside it.

The hippocampus, Ravi said, works rather like a busy librarian who takes the events of each day, files them and helps to send them on to longer-term storage elsewhere in the brain. When it is damaged, as it was in one famous patient who lost parts of both hippocampi in an operation for severe seizures, a person may keep old memories but find it almost impossible to form new lasting ones. The story made Leila shiver, but Ravi pointed out that it also showed how precise the hippocampus's job really is.

Ravi's favourite example was the taxi drivers of London, who spend years memorising thousands of streets and the best routes between them before they are allowed to work. When researchers scanned their brains, they found that the back part of the hippocampus was larger than in other people, and larger still in those who had been driving for longest. A later study that followed trainees found growth in those who qualified but not in those who failed, which made the case stronger.

Like many parts of the body, the hippocampus tends to shrink slowly with age, and in dementia the loss is faster and more severe. This is why researchers have wondered whether regular exercise might slow the shrinkage, and they have tested the question in several ways. Ravi said that the best-known test had begun with a simple walk, much like the one that Leila took each morning.

Ravi described a well-known trial in which about one hundred and twenty older adults were divided at random into two groups, and for a year one group walked three days a week while the other did gentle stretching and toning. At the end, the hippocampus of the walkers had grown by about two percent, whereas that of the stretchers had shrunk by a little over one percent, which is roughly what ageing would predict. It was one of the most hopeful results in the field, and he told it to her slowly so that she would remember it.

Then Ravi did something that Leila was beginning to love in him: he spoiled his own story. Later studies, he said, have given mixed results, with some finding small growth and others finding no change at all, and a larger hippocampus does not automatically mean a sharper memory. The honest summary was that the result was hopeful and interesting, but nowhere near the last word.

The hippocampus has another talent, Ravi said, which is to keep similar memories apart: this morning's parking space, yesterday's parking space and last Tuesday's all look alike, yet the brain must not confuse them. Leila saw at once that this was precisely the trouble with her keys, since she had put them down in a dozen similar places on a dozen similar days. A fixed place for them, he suggested, would spare her brain the sorting altogether, which was far more efficient than trying to become a better detective.

In one small experiment, Ravi said, volunteers learned a set of pictures and then did a session of exercise either straight away, four hours later, or not at all. Two days afterwards, the group who had exercised four hours after learning remembered the most, while those who exercised immediately did no better than those who stayed still. It was an intriguing result, but a single study with a modest number of people could only suggest an idea, and he said that more research was needed before anyone arranged a day around it.

At work on Thursday, Leila began an experiment of her own: she gave every colleague's name a vivid, slightly silly image, so that Marcus became a Mars bar balanced on a tall man's head. Ravi, hearing about it that evening, said that the real secret behind the trick was attention, since nobody can remember a name that was never properly noticed, and the image only forces the noticing. It was not exercise at all, he added, but a good strategy was a good strategy, and he was happy to be proved less important than a chocolate bar.

On Friday morning Leila walked straight to Marcus's desk, said his name aloud and confessed that she had lost it entirely a week before. Marcus burst out laughing and admitted that he forgot names every single day, which was why he kept a list of clients inside his drawer. Leila returned to her own desk lighter than she had felt in months, and it occurred to her that being honest about forgetting might be doing more for her mood than any amount of silent worrying.

Many large surveys, Ravi told her over the noise of the Saturday market, find that people who exercise regularly tend to have better memory and thinking in later life. The difficulty is that active people also differ from inactive ones in countless other ways: they may smoke less, eat better, earn more, have more education and live in safer neighbourhoods, and any of these could be the real cause. Scientists call such hidden extras confounders, and removing their influence is half of the whole business of research.

A second trap is that cause and effect can run in the wrong direction, Ravi said. Someone whose brain has quietly begun to change years before any diagnosis may feel less motivated, walk less and withdraw from activities, so that poor thinking leads to inactivity rather than inactivity leading to poor thinking. Researchers call this reverse causation, and good studies try to get around it by following people for many years or by testing exercise directly.

The fairest way to find out, Ravi said, is a randomised trial, in which a coin toss or a computer decides which volunteers will exercise and which will do something else. Because chance has no preferences, the two groups should start out alike in age, health, wealth and habits, so that any difference at the end is far more likely to be caused by the exercise itself. Leila said it was like auditing a firm's accounts: you pick the samples at random so that nobody can tidy them in advance.

Everything depends on what the comparison group does, Ravi said: they might stretch, attend health talks or simply carry on with their lives. A medicine can be disguised as a dummy pill, but nobody can disguise a brisk walk, so volunteers know their group, and hope or disappointment may colour how hard they try on memory tests. That, he said, is one reason why exercise trials are harder to interpret than drug trials.

When the evidence comes from randomised trials, Ravi said, the picture is more mixed than the surveys suggest, but it is still hopeful. Some trials find modest gains in thinking, whereas others find little or nothing, and the size of any benefit varies with the type of exercise, the length of the trial and the people involved. Leila said that this sounded like a verdict of "not proven," and Ravi, delighted, said that it was a very fair summary.

Scientists try to settle such questions by combining many trials into a single review, but even the reviews do not always agree. One large review of aerobic exercise in healthy older adults found little clear benefit, while others found small gains, partly because they included different exercises, different tests and different people. Ravi said that when experts disagree like this, the sensible reading is that any effect is probably modest, and that nobody should promise more.

Where trials do find a benefit for thinking, Ravi explained, it is usually modest: a small step in the right direction, not a leap from forgetful to brilliant. He asked her to picture a gentle nudge to a bicycle that is already rolling, helpful but not the whole journey. Leila found this oddly reassuring, because miracles had always made her suspicious, and the lack of promises made her trust the rest of what he told her.

There was a further problem, which scientists call publication bias: a study with an exciting result is more likely to be printed than one that finds nothing. The published record can therefore look rosier than the truth, so many researchers now register their plans in advance and publish their results whatever they show. Leila, who had once spent a week hunting for a missing pound in a ledger, said that she knew how tempting it was to leave the awkward numbers out.

Leila put down her notebook and asked the question that had been waiting all week: was all this walking worthwhile if the benefit for the brain was only modest? Ravi replied that exercise also helps the heart, the bones, the mood and the sleep, and that for most people the risks are small. It was worth doing even if the brain effect turned out smaller than anyone hoped, he said, because the brain benefit was a bonus on top of benefits that were already well established.

That night Leila wrote a heading at the top of a clean page, Four Questions, and underneath she listed them: who took part, how many of them were there, compared with what, and how big was the effect? She read them over twice, because they seemed to her useful not only for exercise but for every newspaper headline that had ever frightened or tempted her. Ravi said that if she kept only one thing from the whole month, he would not mind if it were that page.
