On Sunday afternoon Ravi laid three small cards on the table, a chess piece, a clock and a juggler, and explained that each stood for one of the skills that scientists call executive functions. Planning ahead, switching smoothly between tasks and holding attention on what matters are the abilities that run the rest of the mind, he said, like a conductor who plays no instrument. Reviews of exercise trials often find their clearest effects here, rather than in memory itself, although the effects are modest and not found in every study.

To show her what he meant, Ravi laid out a pack of cards on which colour words were printed in clashing ink, so that the word green might appear in red letters. Leila had to name the colour of the ink and ignore the word, and she stumbled again and again, because reading is so automatic that the brain has to hold itself back from doing it. It is a classic known as the Stroop test, he said, and it measures one kind of attention control that tends to tire when we are busy.

The front of the brain, behind the forehead, takes charge of planning and attention, and it is a thirsty region that depends on a good blood supply and on chemical messengers such as dopamine. Exercise changes both, Ravi said, which may be why these skills seem to respond especially well, although this is a reasonable guess and not a proven explanation. Leila wrote the word dopamine in her notebook, then added a question mark, because she was learning that in science a question mark is often the most honest punctuation.

Ravi asked her to describe exactly what had happened on the evening of the zipped pocket, and Leila realised that she had put the keys away while talking to a client, without looking at her hands. In that case, Ravi said, the problem was probably not memory at all but attention, because a memory cannot be stored for something that was never properly noticed. Seen in that light, the keys were less a symptom than a sign that she was doing too many things at once, and that was a difficulty she knew how to solve.

Leila decided to treat the problem as an engineer would, and so she began to say "keys on the hook" aloud each time that she hung them up. Saying it forced a second of real attention, and Ravi told her that a second of attention is often all that a memory needs in order to form. Within a few days, the keys had stopped wandering, and she felt a quiet, private pride that had nothing whatever to do with exercise.

Some of the best-supported findings, Ravi said, concern a single session of exercise: after as little as ten or twenty minutes of moderate activity, many people show a brief improvement in attention and in how quickly they process information. The benefit does not last all day, but it can last long enough to help with a demanding task, so a brisk walk before an exam or a difficult meeting is not a foolish idea. Leila filed the information away for the following Monday, when she had a long set of accounts to finish.

Their route passed a primary school at break time, and a flood of children poured into the playground, shrieking and racing as if they had been bottled up all morning. Ravi told Leila that several school studies have found that pupils pay attention better after a short burst of activity, and that some teachers now build movement into the lessons themselves. He added that the results vary, but that anybody who has ever watched a restless class would not be surprised.

On Monday Leila finished a mountain of accounts a full hour before her usual time, and she walked home with the faint swagger of a woman who has beaten a deadline. She told Ravi that it had to be the effect of the morning walk, but he smiled and reminded her that it could equally have been the quiet office, a good night's sleep or simple luck. It was a data point, he said, and a pleasant one, but a single data point is only the first dot on a graph.

Multitasking is largely a myth, Ravi said, because the brain cannot give full attention to two demanding things at the same time; it merely jumps back and forth, and each jump costs a little time and accuracy. Leila thought about the telephone clamped between her ear and shoulder while she typed, and about all the half-formed memories that must have slipped away in those moments. She resolved to do one thing at a time, even if it made her look old-fashioned, and was relieved to learn that doing less at once might be the quickest way to remember more.

That evening it was Ravi's turn to be defeated: he stared at the same paragraph of his project for an hour and typed nothing at all. Leila, who had been told a great deal about attention that week, handed him his coat and said "Walk," and twenty minutes later he came back with the paragraph already written in his head. He admitted cheerfully that a single walk proved nothing, but he also admitted that he had not solved a problem so quickly in weeks, and Leila wrote the date in her notebook.

On Tuesday, after half an hour of brisk walking in cold, bright air, Leila stopped on the towpath and spread her arms wide like a child pretending to be an aeroplane. She felt lighter and calmer than she had for weeks, as though a heavy coat had been taken off her shoulders, and she asked Ravi what on earth was happening inside her. He said that exercise is one of the things that often changes mood, and he promised that the explanation was more complicated than anyone had expected.

One of the best-known answers, Ravi said, is endorphins, which are chemicals that the body makes to ease pain and which are also linked with pleasure. Exercise seems to release them, and brain scans of runners have shown signs of this release in areas that deal with emotion, which may help to explain the so-called runner's high. Yet few people feel anything so dramatic on a gentle walk, so he suspected that endorphins were only part of the story.

Other chemicals are almost certainly involved, Ravi said, including dopamine, which is tied to motivation and reward, serotonin, which is tied to mood, and a family of molecules called endocannabinoids that the body makes naturally. The chemistry of the brain, he said, is a crowded kitchen in which dozens of cooks stir the same pots at once, and nobody has yet worked out which of them matters most in people. Leila said that she preferred a kitchen with fewer cooks, and he agreed that science would be much simpler if the brain had listened to her.

Chemistry is only part of the explanation, Ravi added, because a walk offers fresh air, daylight, steady rhythm, a change of scenery and the quiet satisfaction of having done something difficult. Psychologists argue that a feeling of achievement may be just as important as any molecule, and it costs nothing at all. Leila reflected that the idea of simply walking her worries into a better shape had never once occurred to her.

Stress has its own chemistry, Ravi said, and its chief character is cortisol, a hormone that rises when we face a challenge and helps the body to mobilise its energy. During exercise cortisol rises briefly, which sounds like a contradiction, but afterwards it settles, and some studies suggest that regular exercise makes the whole stress response less sharp over time. He cautioned that the findings are not uniform, and that the rise during a workout is a normal part of how the body copes with effort, not a sign of harm.

The stress response evolved for emergencies such as an animal in the grass, Ravi said, and it prepares the body to fight or flee by speeding the heart and flooding the muscles with fuel. Modern worries, like an unpaid invoice or an angry email, trigger the same machinery, yet we respond by sitting perfectly still, so the energy has nowhere to go. A brisk walk gives the body what it was preparing for, and many people notice that their restlessness settles as a result.

On Wednesday a deadline loomed over the office like a grey cloud, and Leila did something she had never done before: she put on her coat at lunchtime and walked briskly round Market square instead of eating at her desk. Marcus saw her pass the window, grabbed his own coat and caught her up, and by the second lap he was laughing at his own jokes. They came back to their desks looking pink and slightly foolish, and the afternoon's work went more easily than either of them had expected.

On Thursday morning Ravi taught her a simple trick: breathe in for four steps and out for four, and keep it up for a few minutes. Slow, steady breathing seems to calm the body's alarm system, and the counting gives a busy mind something small to hold on to, which is why many forms of meditation use it. Leila tried it along the towpath, lost count at least five times, and found at the end of the lap that her shoulders had dropped half an inch.

Anxiety is a different matter from everyday stress, Ravi said, but studies suggest that regular exercise can reduce its symptoms for many people. Exercise is not a cure, and anyone whose anxiety is severe or lasts a long time deserves proper help from a doctor or a therapist. Leila, who was not anxious in that way, listened with the attention of a woman who knew several people who were.

By the end of the week Leila had started a mood diary, in which she scored her feelings from one to five before and after every walk and added a line about the weather. Ravi told her that feelings are not proof of anything, because hope can sway them, but that a record kept honestly for weeks is useful information, and far better than trusting her memory. She drew a tiny face beside each score, and the faces, she noticed, were beginning to smile more often.

On Sunday evening Ravi's voice grew quieter as he came to a more serious subject, which was depression. Reviews of many trials, he said, find that exercise can reduce the symptoms of mild to moderate depression, although the quality of the studies varies and the size of the effect differs from one analysis to another. But he stressed, more than once, that exercise is not a replacement for professional care, and that nobody should try to walk their way out of a serious illness alone.

Depression, Ravi explained, is far more than a bad day: it is a low mood that lasts for weeks, often together with a loss of interest in things once enjoyed, poor sleep, altered appetite and exhaustion. It can also make concentration difficult, which means that a person who is depressed may easily believe that their memory is failing, when what has really been affected is their attention. Leila listened very quietly, because some of the signs were uncomfortably familiar from the winter after her mother's funeral.

There are several reasons why exercise might lift a low mood, Ravi said, and nobody knows how much each one counts. It gets a person out of the house and into daylight, it interrupts the circling of brooding thoughts, it often brings company, and it can improve sleep, which is often disturbed in depression. Together, he suggested, these small gains may add up to something larger than any of them alone, in the way that many small stitches make a coat.

One piece of advice mattered more than all the rest, Ravi said: if low mood lasts two weeks or more, or makes ordinary life difficult, a person should talk to a doctor. Effective help is available, and if someone ever has thoughts of harming themselves, they should contact an emergency service or a crisis line at once, and not wait. He did not say it as a lecture but as a plain fact, and Leila copied it into her notebook in capital letters.

The cruel difficulty, Ravi said, is that exercise feels hardest at exactly the moment when it might help most, because low mood drains energy and makes every effort seem pointless. The trick that therapists suggest is to start so small that it feels almost silly, perhaps ten minutes outside, since motivation often follows action rather than leading it. If the ten minutes become five, he said, that still counts, and the only unforgivable thing is to call it failure.

On Monday evening Leila's old friend Joan called round, and she looked a good deal thinner and greyer than she had at the summer fair. She said that she had felt flat since retiring in the spring, that she had no energy for anything and that there seemed no point in going out. Ravi, to his credit, did not give a lecture, and Leila only asked whether Joan would walk with her as far as the corner and back, which Joan, after a long pause, agreed to do.

Later that evening, over a mug of tea that went cold, Leila admitted something she had not said even to herself. In the winter after her mother died she had slept badly, eaten little and let a hundred small things slide, and she suspected that the forgetfulness had started then. Ravi said that grief is exhausting for the mind as well as the heart, and that difficulty with concentration and memory is common for a long while afterwards, which did not mean that something was wrong with her.

Worry, Ravi pointed out, has a cost of its own, because a mind that is busy rehearsing its fears has less attention left over for the task in hand. The more Leila dreaded forgetting, the more likely she was to forget, since the dread occupied the very space in which new information needed to settle. It was a vicious circle, he said, but one that could be broken from either end, by calming the worry or by practising the habits that make forgetting less likely.

After two weeks Leila added up her mood diary, and the pattern was plain: the score after a walk beat the score before it on all but two occasions, often by a point or more. Ravi pointed out, with a smile, that this was a small personal record and not a trial, but he said that in a month she would know better what suited her than any survey could tell her. "Your brain is not broken," he added gently, "it is only busy and tired, and it is doing its best."

On another grey, dripping Sunday, Leila stayed on the sofa with a blanket and a book she did not read, and her mood score in the notebook was the lowest of the month. Ravi did not scold her, but said that feelings rise and fall like the weather and that a single flat day is not a failure, only a day. They agreed on a minimum walk for such moments, just ten minutes round the block, and she did it in the rain at four o'clock and wrote down a three instead of a one.

On Tuesday the towpath ran for half a mile beneath a tunnel of old trees whose leaves had turned to copper, and Leila felt her shoulders drop before she had noticed they were raised. Ravi said that many people describe walks among trees and grass as calming, and that surveys link green surroundings with better wellbeing. How much of this is the greenery itself, and how much is the quiet, the clean air and the lack of traffic, is a question that researchers are still trying to untangle.

Ravi described a small study in which volunteers walked for ninety minutes, half of them through a park-like area of grass and trees and half beside a busy road. Afterwards the nature walkers said that they spent less time brooding over their problems, and a brain scan showed less activity in an area linked with that kind of repetitive worry. The group was small and the study was brief, he cautioned, so it was an interesting hint and not a rule.

One theory, which Ravi described with an almost visible shrug, holds that natural scenes such as moving leaves, rippling water and birds in flight attract our attention gently and without effort. A city street demands constant, deliberate focus, whereas a hedgerow lets the focusing system rest, and a rested system may work better afterwards. The idea is attractive and has some support, but the results are mixed, so he put it firmly in the category of interesting rather than settled.

As the sun rose over the lock gates, Ravi explained that the body keeps an internal clock, known as the circadian rhythm, which runs for roughly twenty-four hours and is set mainly by light entering the eyes. Daylight in the morning tells the brain that the day has begun, which helps to fix the times of sleepiness and alertness and so affects how well we sleep at night. That, he said, was one more small advantage of walking outdoors rather than staying in all day.

Sunlight on the skin also allows the body to make vitamin D, which is needed for healthy bones and muscles and may have other roles that are still being studied. In the northern winter, when the sun is low and the days are short, many people make very little, so some health services advise a supplement for part of the year. Whether that applies to any one person, Ravi said firmly, was a matter for a doctor or a pharmacist, and not for a student on a canal path.

By the third week the weather had turned, and the leaves lay in golden drifts along the canal while a thin wind blew from the north. Leila bought a warm hat and a pair of gloves, and she learned to dress in layers that could be peeled off as her body warmed, which Ravi said was the whole secret of walking through the cold. He quoted a saying that there is no such thing as bad weather, only the wrong clothes, and it irritated her mildly to find that it was true.

Some researchers have begun to study what they call blue space, meaning rivers, lakes, coasts and canals, and a few studies link living or walking near water with better wellbeing. The research is still young, and it is hard to separate the effect of the water from that of the paths and the people around it. Leila, watching a moorhen tiptoe across the floating leaves, decided that she did not need a controlled trial to know that the canal had become her favourite place in the world.

Not everyone has a canal on the doorstep, and Ravi was careful to say that nobody should feel shut out of the benefits by the street they live in. A small park, a row of street trees, a garden square or even plants on a windowsill can supply a modest dose of green, and any of these is better than none at all. Leila thought of Joan's flat above the chemist's, with its single geranium, and made a mental note to take her to the little park on Church Street.

One more factor deserves a mention, Ravi said as a lorry thundered along the main road: air pollution, which expert reviews now list among the factors linked with a higher risk of dementia. The evidence shows a link and not a proof, and the effect for any single person is small, but the practical lesson is simple enough. Where there is a choice, walk along quiet streets, parks and paths, and leave the busy ring road to the lorries.

At the end of the week Ravi asked her to stop in the middle of the path and name five things that she could see, then four that she could hear and three that she could feel. A grey heron stood at the edge of the water, motionless as a statue, and Leila found that she had forgotten her worries for a whole minute while she watched it. Paying quiet, deliberate attention is a skill that can be trained, he said, and it is one that helps both a wandering mind and a hurried one.

After more than two weeks of morning walks, Leila noticed something that she had stopped expecting: she fell asleep within minutes of turning off the lamp and woke only once in the night, instead of three or four times. Ravi said that this fitted what researchers had seen, since exercise tends to improve sleep, and sleep is one of the best friends that memory has. He suggested that, in the next few days, they should look more closely at what happens inside the head after dark.

Sleep is not a blank, Ravi told her, but a busy night shift during which the brain sorts the day's material. In deep sleep the hippocampus appears to replay the patterns of activity from recent events, and this helps to move them into longer-term storage in the outer layers of the brain, a process known as consolidation. A person who sleeps badly after learning something new, he said, gives that process much less chance to work.

Experiments in mice have suggested that the spaces around brain cells widen during sleep, allowing fluid to wash away waste products more efficiently than in the waking state. Researchers are studying whether the same process happens in people, and whether it matters for diseases such as Alzheimer's, but the answers are not in yet and nobody should claim them. Leila smiled at the image of a gentle tide washing through her head every night, and decided that she would rather like to be in bed on time.

Most adults need somewhere between seven and nine hours of sleep a night, Ravi said, although individuals differ a little. Leila had been getting five or six throughout the long weeks of the tax returns, and he explained that even a modest shortage of sleep reduces attention, slows thinking and makes it harder to form new memories the following day. She looked guiltily at her old habit of answering emails until midnight, and he gently told her that nobody was perfect, and that the aim was progress and not blame.

Reviews of many studies, Ravi said, generally agree that regular exercise improves sleep, although the improvement is modest rather than miraculous. People who exercise tend to fall asleep a little faster, to spend more time in deep sleep and to feel less sleepy during the day, and the effect seems to be present at every age, including older age. Better sleep may in turn help memory, mood and attention, so the benefits of the walks could be quietly supporting one another.

Timing seems to matter less than people fear, Ravi said: studies suggest that most people sleep perfectly well after exercising in the evening, although a few feel wide awake after hard effort close to bedtime. His advice was to experiment, to notice what suits the body and to remember that gentle exercise before bed, such as a slow stroll, is unlikely to cause trouble. Leila, who had always assumed that the answer was one fixed rule, felt oddly freed by this permission to find her own.

Ravi then offered a short list of ordinary habits that help most people to sleep. Caffeine stays in the body for many hours, so a late coffee can steal the night, and alcohol may bring sleep quickly but makes it lighter and more broken. Bright screens in the last hour can keep the brain in daytime mode, while a dark, cool and quiet bedroom is the cheapest sleeping aid ever invented.

On Saturday afternoon Leila fell asleep on the sofa, and woke after twenty minutes feeling extraordinarily refreshed. Ravi said that short naps of that length may restore alertness for many people, but that long naps, or naps taken late in the afternoon, can make it harder to sleep at night. He added that someone who is sleepy all day, every day, despite a full night in bed, should mention it to a doctor and not simply reach for another coffee.

That evening Ravi fell asleep on the sofa with his laptop balanced on his chest and snored so loudly that the china rattled in the dresser, and Leila took a photograph to use against him later. When he woke up, he explained that snoring is very often harmless, but that loud snoring with pauses in breathing, together with heavy tiredness by day, can be a sign of a condition called sleep apnoea. It can be tested and treated, he said, which is exactly why it is worth mentioning to a doctor.

Leila added a new column to her diary, in which she noted her bedtime, the number of times she woke and how rested she felt in the morning. Within a week she was averaging nearly seven hours, and the habit that had cost her most, answering emails at midnight, had been replaced by a cup of camomile tea and ten pages of a novel. Ravi studied the chart with great satisfaction, although he reminded her that it was a record of habits and not a proof of cause.

When Leila added up a typical working day, she was shocked to find that she sat down for almost eight hours, not counting the bus and the evening sofa. Ravi said that researchers use the word sedentary for this kind of long, still sitting, and that large studies link it with a higher risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and early death. These are links and not proofs, he added, and the numbers vary, but the pattern appears again and again across different countries.

Sitting less and exercising more are two different habits, Ravi explained, and each seems to matter in its own right. A good morning walk reduces the risks of a sedentary day, and some studies suggest that a great deal of activity can offset most of them, but it does not entirely cancel eight hours in a chair. The good news, he said, was that the remedy for sitting was cheap, easy and available to anyone with a pair of legs.

The next morning Leila set her telephone to ring every thirty minutes, and each time it sounded she stood up and did something small, such as filling the kettle. Her colleagues stared for the first day, and by the end of the week two of them had set timers of their own. Ravi, hearing the news, said that the best habits are the ones that spread by themselves.

Several small laboratory studies, Ravi said, have asked volunteers to sit for long periods, interrupting the sitting in some sessions with a few minutes of gentle walking. After meals the walkers had steadier blood sugar and, in some of the studies, lower blood pressure, which is relevant to the brain because both blood sugar and blood pressure affect its small vessels. The studies were short and the groups were small, he reminded her, but they fitted with the larger picture and cost nothing to follow.

One small study that Ravi had read scanned adults between forty-five and seventy-five, and those who sat longer each day had a thinner section of the temporal lobe, an area that supports memory. The study involved only a few dozen people and measured sitting by questionnaire, so it showed a link, not a cause. He mentioned it, he said, not as a warning but as one piece of a pattern that kept pointing in the same direction.

Marcus had a standing desk, and Leila wondered aloud whether she should ask the firm for one. Ravi replied that standing burns slightly more energy than sitting and may be kinder to the back, but that standing perfectly still for hours is tiring in its own way and is no substitute for walking. The best advice, he said, was to vary the day, alternating sitting, standing and moving, since the real enemy was not the chair but the long period without a change.

Marcus, now a keen walker, proposed that they hold their weekly planning meeting on foot, and the two of them strolled round Market square with a notebook and a takeaway coffee instead of sitting in the stuffy meeting room. Ravi told her afterwards that a small study at a university in California found that people produced more creative ideas while walking than while sitting, though he warned that the study was small and the task was narrow. Leila said that it hardly mattered, because the meeting had ended in twenty minutes instead of an hour and nobody had yawned.

In the evenings, Leila made a game of the television: whenever the advertisements came on, she stood up and marched on the spot, rose on her toes or climbed the stairs once. It felt ridiculous at first, and Ravi laughed so much that he missed the end of his programme, but she pointed out that eight breaks an evening came to a surprising amount of movement. Light activity of this kind, he conceded, counts for something, and for people who cannot manage more it may be a perfectly good place to begin.

It turned out that the expert was as guilty as anyone, because Ravi's back had begun to ache after weeks of hunching over his laptop at the kitchen table. Leila, with some satisfaction, proposed a rule for the pair of them: stand up every half hour, and take a proper ten-minute walk every two hours. They shook hands on it for the second time that month, and Ravi remarked that he had never before been held to account by someone so skilled with a spreadsheet.

Leila borrowed Ravi's step counter for a day, and the figure at bedtime was a sobering one: only about three thousand steps on an ordinary office day, without the canal walk. She did not resolve to leap straight to some heroic total but to add a few hundred steps each week, which Ravi said is exactly how people who succeed tend to do it. The number on the little screen, she noticed, had turned a vague worry into a plain fact that she could do something about, and that was a relief.

On Tuesday evening Ravi pulled up the guidelines of the World Health Organization, which advise adults to aim for between one hundred and fifty and three hundred minutes of moderate activity every week. That is between two and a half and five hours, he pointed out, and it sounds far more alarming when it is written as a total than when it is spread across seven days of ordinary life. Leila, who had expected a number of Olympic proportions, found that her morning walks had carried her past the lower figure already.

The guidelines also allow for harder effort, Ravi said, since seventy-five to one hundred and fifty minutes of vigorous activity can meet the same target. As a rough rule, a minute of vigorous activity counts for about two minutes of moderate activity, and a mixture of the two is perfectly acceptable. Vigorous activity, he added, is not needed to gain many of the benefits, and it is not the right choice for everyone, so there is no shame in staying with the walking.

On Wednesday Leila asked how anyone could tell moderate effort from vigorous effort without a laboratory, and Ravi answered that the talk test was all she needed. At a moderate pace you can hold a conversation but not sing, whereas at a vigorous pace you can manage only a few words before you need to breathe. They tried it the next morning, humming a tune all the way along the canal and gasping through the chorus whenever the path climbed.

The minutes do not have to arrive in a single block, Ravi said, because the current guidelines count activity of any length towards the weekly total, so three brisk ten-minute walks equal one long stroll. A person who cannot find half an hour in a busy day can therefore collect it in pieces, on the stairs, on the way to the shop or round the block at lunchtime. Leila smiled, because her half-hour timer and her lunchtime laps had already been doing exactly that without her knowing the rule.

Ravi enjoyed telling her that the famous target of ten thousand steps began in the nineteen-sixties as the name of a Japanese pedometer, said to have been chosen because the character for ten thousand looks like a walking figure. Later research suggests that the link with a lower risk of early death levels off at roughly six to eight thousand steps a day for older adults, and a little higher for younger ones. For the brain itself, he admitted, nobody knows the ideal number, but the pattern suggests that moving more is better than moving less, up to a point.

One of the most encouraging patterns in the research, Ravi said, is that the biggest gains in health tend to come when the least active people begin to move a little. The step from doing nothing to doing something is larger than the step from a great deal to even more, which means that no one needs to feel they have started too late or too slowly. Leila, who had spent most of her adult life believing that she was not an exercising kind of person, discovered that the evidence was cheerfully on the side of people exactly like her.

Ravi taught her another measure that required no equipment, which was a scale of effort from zero, meaning sitting still, to ten, meaning the hardest effort she could possibly manage. Moderate activity, he said, feels like a five or six, while vigorous activity feels like a seven or eight, and the scale works for people of any fitness because it measures how hard the effort feels to them. That evening Leila rated her morning walk at six and felt rather like a scientist, which delighted both of them.

Leila wondered whether she should simply do more and more, but Ravi shook his head and said that the relationship is not a straight line. After a certain point the benefits become small, and it is not clear that very large amounts do more for the brain than moderate ones, while hard exercise without rest can cause injury. Rest days, he said, are not laziness but part of training, because it is during recovery that muscles repair themselves and the body adapts.

On Sunday evening Leila added up her week, and the sum made her sit up straight: seven morning walks, plus lunchtime laps and timer breaks, came to well over two hundred minutes. It was more than the minimum that the experts recommend, and she had reached it without once buying special clothes or paying for a membership. The question that now troubled her was not whether she could do it for a month, but whether she would do it when Ravi had gone home.

For years Leila had believed that exercise meant a gym, with its mirrors, its machines and its air of competition, and she had once paid for a membership that she used exactly twice. Ravi told her that a gym is a fine place for people who enjoy it and want equipment, but that walking, dancing and gardening all count as activity, and none of them requires a subscription. A pair of comfortable shoes and a safe path, he said, were all the apparatus that the human brain had ever asked for.

Walking was only half of the advice, Ravi said, because the guidelines also recommend muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days a week. In the kitchen he handed Leila two full bottles of water and showed her how to lift them slowly, and within a minute her arms were trembling in a way that astonished her. She had assumed that weights were for young men in vests, and found that they were also for women of fifty-five with a bottle in each hand.

From about the middle of life, Ravi explained, the body gradually loses muscle unless that muscle is used, a process with the grand name of sarcopenia. The loss tends to speed up in later years, and since muscle is what lifts a person from a chair, carries the shopping and keeps the legs steady, losing it affects far more than appearance. The encouraging part, he said, is that muscle responds to training at any age, including the eighties and nineties.

Muscles are not just machinery, Ravi told her, because working muscles release chemical messengers called myokines into the bloodstream, and some of these may influence other organs. Whether any of them reach the brain in amounts that matter is being studied, with intriguing results in animals and cautious ones in people, so he described the research as young and exciting rather than established. Muscles seem to speak to the brain, he said, but scientists are still learning the language.

Reviews of trials in older adults have found that regular resistance training, in which muscles work against weights or their own body weight, may modestly improve some thinking skills, particularly planning and attention. The gains are small and the results are not identical from study to study, Ravi said, so the evidence is still developing. Leila noted that the muscles were being asked to do something quite different from walking, and that this variety might itself be a virtue.

The guidelines ask for all the major muscle groups to be worked on two or more days a week, Ravi said, and that does not require a gym or even a great deal of space. Standing up from a chair, pressing against a wall, rising onto the toes and lifting bottles are enough to begin with, and each can be done in the kitchen while the kettle boils. Leila drew up a little list, with ten repetitions of each, and stuck it to the refrigerator door.

Her first attempt at ten chair stands ended with a wobble at the seventh, a shriek of laughter at the eighth and a heroic collapse into the seat at the tenth. Ravi told her cheerfully that a little struggle is the whole point, because muscles adapt only when asked to do slightly more than usual, and that the exercise would feel easier soon. She tried again that evening, and then again the next morning, secretly competing against the weaker woman she had been the day before.

Ravi insisted on a few safety rules before she went any further: move slowly and with control, breathe out on the effort, and never hold the breath. Begin with light weights and add a little at a time, he said, because a mild ache the next day is normal but a sharp pain is a signal to stop. Anyone with joint, heart or blood pressure problems should ask a doctor or a physiotherapist before starting, and he said it so earnestly that Leila almost saluted.

Within two weeks the bottles had become too easy, so Leila swapped them for two bags of rice from the cupboard, which made her feel like a weightlifter at the supermarket. Ravi named the principle behind this, which is that muscles grow stronger when they are asked for a little more than before, whether by extra repetitions, a heavier weight or a slower movement. The key is gradual progress, he said, because a sudden jump is the quickest route to an injury.

Bones are living tissue, Ravi explained, and like muscles they respond to demands, growing denser when muscles pull on them and the feet strike the ground firmly. This matters especially for women of Leila's age, since bone is lost faster in the years after the menopause, and a doctor can advise on bone health and on whether any tests or supplements are appropriate. Strong bones, he said, were another reason to like a weekly strength routine, even though they were a bonus outside the brain.

On Saturday Leila carried two heavy bags of shopping from the market all the way up her front steps, and she noticed with some astonishment that she was neither puffing nor sore. Ravi said that such everyday abilities, standing up from a chair, climbing stairs and carrying a bag, are what strength is really for, and that they help people to stay independent as the years pass. She stood in the hallway among the bags with a feeling that she had not had since she was young, which was the pleasure of being strong.

On Thursday evening Leila walked into the community hall for the first time since a cousin's wedding, with Ravi beside her to watch from a chair by the wall. The teacher, Nadia, a small energetic woman in silver trainers, lined up a dozen neighbours and taught them a single simple step, which they repeated to a tune from the radio until it began to feel like a pattern. Leila's feet were hopelessly slow at first, but the room was so cheerful that she forgot to be embarrassed.

In the interval, Ravi pointed out that dancing is a clever kind of exercise, because it combines several different demands in a single activity. The heart works harder, the memory holds a sequence of steps, the ears follow a beat, the eyes watch the neighbours, and the whole thing happens in company, to music, which many people find uplifting. It is hard to design a better workout for the brain, he said, although nobody can yet prove that dance is better than other kinds of exercise.

Ravi described a small but famous study in which adults who had never juggled were taught the skill, and brain scans after three months showed growth in areas that process visual movement. When the volunteers stopped practising, those changes shrank again over the next three months, which suggests that the brain keeps what it uses and gradually lets go of what it does not. It was a neat demonstration, he said, of plasticity at work, though the numbers were small and the changes were measured in tiny amounts.

A small German study followed older adults for eighteen months, with some of them learning dance routines that grew harder and others doing standard fitness training. Parts of the hippocampus grew in both groups, which is encouraging, but only the dancers showed a clear improvement in balance, perhaps because their routines kept changing and demanded constant attention. Ravi called it suggestive and not decisive, since the groups were small, and he would not claim that dance was a magic ingredient.

A new, faster step defeated Leila completely: she trod on her own foot, bumped gently into a neighbour and lost the beat three times, while Nadia clapped louder and called out that nobody was watching. Ravi said afterwards that learning psychologists have a name for this, desirable difficulty, which means that tasks that feel slightly too hard often lead to deeper and longer-lasting learning than tasks that feel easy. A mistake, in other words, was not a sign that her brain was failing but one of the ways in which it was being exercised.

Music, Ravi explained, tends to make exercise feel easier, partly by distracting the mind from effort and partly because a steady beat encourages a steady pace. He compiled a playlist of songs for walking, carefully chosen for their rhythm, and Leila promptly spoiled the scheme by adding a dozen of her own favourites from the nineteen-eighties. The tempo of the tunes turned out to matter less than her enjoyment of them, and she found that she could walk for half an hour before she thought of looking at her watch.

Leila had done the crossword every morning for twenty years, and she asked Ravi whether it was protecting her memory. Brain-training games reliably make people better at those games, he said, but the evidence that the skill carries over to everyday life is weaker than the advertisements suggest, and scientists still disagree about how far. Learning something truly new, such as a language, an instrument or a craft, asks the brain to build a wider range of connections, so he suggested that she keep the crossword for pleasure and add a challenge.

With Ravi's encouragement, Leila signed up for a beginners' Spanish class that met on Tuesday evenings in the library, and she turned up with a new pencil and a stomach full of butterflies. The first lesson was full of laughter and mispronunciations, and she came home with a page of new words and the delighted conviction that she had been wrong about her brain's willingness to try. Ravi, who spoke only enough Spanish to order a coffee, promised to be her first and most patient conversation partner.

One morning a storm made the towpath too slippery for walking, so Leila turned up the radio, kicked off her slippers and danced around the kitchen until the kettle boiled. Afterwards she climbed the stairs six times, to Ravi's great amusement, and he joined her for the last two with a wooden spoon for a microphone. Exercise could happen anywhere, he said, even in a kitchen on a wet Monday, and the body had no idea whether the floor beneath it belonged to a gym or a kitchen.

Nadia was firm that dancing belongs to every body, and she pointed to the corner of the hall where four people were enjoying the same music from their chairs, waving their arms and tapping their feet. The following Friday the hall held a small social evening, and Leila, who would once have hidden behind the tea urn, danced three songs in a row. A courtly neighbour named Mr Hughes asked her for a fourth, dancing with his walking stick hooked over his arm, and she walked home without once thinking about her memory.

On Saturday morning a line of people in the park were moving through a series of slow, flowing gestures, as though pushing against a gentle tide, and Leila stopped at the railings to watch. Their teacher, a woman of at least seventy, shifted her weight from foot to foot with a grace that made the movements look effortless, and her pupils followed with serious faces. It was tai chi, Ravi whispered, and the reason it was slow was that slowness is far harder than it looks.

Tai chi, Ravi explained, began in China as a martial art and is now practised mostly as a gentle form of exercise, combining slow movement, careful shifts of weight and steady breathing. Trials in older people have found that it improves balance and may reduce the number of falls, and there are hints of benefits for mood and for some thinking skills, although those results are less consistent. For people who find vigorous exercise difficult, he said, it is one of the better-studied alternatives.

Yoga, Ravi said, is another gentle option that combines stretching, strength, balance and controlled breathing, and reviews of trials suggest that it can improve flexibility, balance and mood. There are many styles, ranging from slow and restful to vigorous and demanding, and so the sensible course is to choose one that suits the body and to start with a beginners' class. Leila tried a short video on Sunday, discovered that she could not touch her toes, and was told firmly by her nephew that nobody had asked her to.

Ravi proposed an exercise that required neither time nor equipment: stand on one leg while brushing your teeth, keeping a hand near the sink for safety, and change legs halfway through. Balance, he explained, is a skill that fades if it is not used, but it responds quickly to practice, and a minute here and there adds up to a surprising amount over a week. Leila wobbled so wildly on the first morning that she nearly swallowed the toothpaste, but by Friday she could keep her balance for the whole two minutes.

Falls are common, Ravi said: roughly one in three people over the age of sixty-five falls at least once a year, and while most falls cause no serious harm, some lead to broken bones or a loss of confidence. There is also a link with the brain, because a serious blow to the head is among the factors that experts associate with a higher risk of dementia later in life. Strength and balance training reduce the chance of falling, so the kitchen exercises and the toothbrush routine were quietly doing double duty.

Staying upright, Ravi explained, is a surprisingly complicated task that the brain performs without being asked, by combining signals from the inner ear, the eyes, the muscles and the nerves in the soles of the feet. Each of these sources can weaken with age, but the brain is skilful at compensating, and practice improves its coordination of what is left. That, he said, was why standing on one leg in the bathroom was not a joke but a small piece of serious training.

Ravi timed her one evening with his phone while she stood on one leg beside the kitchen counter, ready to grab it if she wobbled. She managed a respectable time on her left foot but only a few seconds on her right, which made them both laugh and then think. Sides often differ, he said, so she would practise a little more on the weaker one, and anyone who is often dizzy or unsteady, he added, should mention it to a doctor.

On the towpath Leila met Mr Hughes, the courtly dancer of the Friday social, and he told her that he swam at the leisure centre twice a week and had done so ever since his knees had begun to complain. Water carries much of the body's weight, Ravi explained afterwards, so swimming and water exercise are kind to sore joints, and they can still raise the heart rate. It is a good example of the principle, he said, that the best exercise is the one a person can actually do.

Ravi also recommended a short warm-up before the longer walks and the strength exercises: about five minutes of easy marching, arm swings and gentle knee lifts to raise the temperature of the muscles and prepare the heart for effort. The evidence that stretching prevents injuries is mixed, he said, so he would not make big promises about it, but most people find that a warm-up and some easy stretching afterwards make the exercise feel more comfortable. Leila noticed that the first stiff minutes of each morning walk had indeed become friendlier since she had begun.

Mr Hughes had a walking stick, a heart tablet in his pocket and a dog called Biscuit, and he said that he never allowed any of them to stop him from walking along the canal every afternoon. Ravi added that exercise can be adapted for almost any body, including people with long-term illness, limited mobility or a wheelchair, and that a doctor or physiotherapist can advise on safe ways to begin. The principle, he said, was not to compare oneself with anyone else but to start from where one is.

From the following Monday, Mr Hughes and Biscuit joined the morning walk, and the little party grew louder, slower and a great deal more cheerful. Biscuit stopped at every second tree, which gave Mr Hughes time to tell stories from thirty years as a postman, and Leila laughed more on that path than in a month at the office. Ravi observed that walking and talking with other people adds a social benefit to the physical one, and that the two seemed to work well together.

Ravi said that loneliness and social isolation are among the factors that expert groups link with a higher risk of dementia, as well as with poorer physical health. The link probably runs in both directions, he added, since people who feel unwell or confused may withdraw from company, and researchers are still working out how much each direction matters. What is clear is that being connected with others is good for wellbeing, and there is no downside to a friendly conversation.

Researchers have proposed an idea called cognitive reserve, Ravi explained, which holds that education, interesting work, lifelong learning and a lively social life may build up a store of resilience in the brain. A brain with plenty of reserve might continue to function well for longer even when some damage has occurred, in the way that a town with many roads can keep traffic moving after one bridge is closed. It remains a theory, however, and he did not want Leila to treat it as a promise.

Even an ordinary chat, Ravi pointed out, is a demanding mental task, because the listener must follow the thread, remember what was said, think of a reply and read the speaker's face. Seen in that light, a morning of conversation with Mr Hughes was a more complete workout than any crossword. Leila said that she had never before thought of gossip as a form of training, and Ravi said that he would not put it in his thesis.

After three attempts Leila persuaded Joan to join the morning walk, and she arrived at the lock in a heavy coat and a woollen hat, looking as though she expected to be sent home. They went slowly, and for the first five minutes she hardly spoke, but by the tenth she was commenting on the ducks and had stopped looking at her feet. When they turned back, she said in a small voice that she felt a little better, and Leila, who had learned a great deal that month, did not make a speech about it.

Ravi had found, on his phone, that the town's park held a free community event every Saturday morning, in which runners, joggers and walkers set off together and finished with coffee at a cafe. Leila, Joan and Mr Hughes went along with Biscuit, and discovered that the walkers outnumbered the runners and that nobody at all was timing anyone. There is something about a crowd of strangers all heading in the same direction, Leila thought, that makes a difficult thing feel easy.

Research on exercise habits suggests that people who train with others tend to keep going for longer than those who go alone, and the reasons are not mysterious. A walking partner provides encouragement, a little gentle accountability and the simple pleasure of company, and it is far harder to stay in bed when a friend is standing at the door with a dog. Leila discovered the truth of this on a freezing Wednesday, when it was only the thought of Mr Hughes waiting in the cold that got her out of bed.

When Nadia confessed that the hall's accounts were a nightmare of shoeboxes and crumpled receipts, Leila heard herself offering to put them in order, and was astonished by how eager she was to begin. Ravi said that studies link purposeful activities, such as volunteering, with better wellbeing and, in some research, with a lower risk of decline in thinking, although it is hard to be sure which comes first. For Leila the evidence mattered less than the feeling of being useful, and she spent three happy evenings with a calculator and a mountain of receipts.

Studies have found that people who own dogs tend to walk more than those who do not, and Mr Hughes was the living proof, because Biscuit needed two long outings a day whatever the weather. He called the animal his personal trainer, a stern and hairy employee who never took a day off and never accepted an excuse. Leila, who had once thought a dog would tie her down, began to wonder whether being tied to something that insisted on fresh air might be the best arrangement of all.

Over coffee at the Lock Cafe, Leila called Joan by Mr Hughes's name and then, trying to put it right, called the dog Marcus, and the whole table dissolved into laughter. Nobody minded in the slightest, and Leila realised that a year earlier she would have blushed and said nothing for the rest of the morning. Ravi remarked quietly that shame about forgetting often does more harm than the forgetting itself, since it makes people hide, and hiding is exactly what gets in the way of friendship and of help.

On a Sunday afternoon Ravi came at last to the question that had been in the background all month. Large studies that follow people for many years, he said, find that those who are physically active have a lower risk of dementia, in some reviews by roughly a quarter. It is a link and not a guarantee, and the cautions of the previous weeks apply: active people differ in many ways, and early illness can itself reduce activity.

Dementia, Ravi explained, is not a single disease but a name for a group of conditions in which memory and thinking decline enough to interfere with everyday life, such as managing money, finding the way home or following a conversation. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause, followed by vascular dementia, which is linked to damage to the blood vessels of the brain. It is not a normal part of getting older, he said, and Leila, who had nursed her mother through it, nodded slowly because she knew exactly what he meant.

Ravi took out a list and explained that an international commission of experts, writing in a medical journal called the Lancet, had gathered the evidence on factors that might change the risk of dementia. They named about fourteen of them, among them blood pressure, hearing loss, smoking, education, depression, inactivity and social contact, and they estimated that nearly half of cases worldwide might in theory be delayed or prevented. He added at once that the figure is an estimate with plenty of uncertainty, and that nobody can tell any individual what their own share would be.

Hearing loss in midlife, Ravi said, is one of the largest items on the list, and researchers are studying whether treating it with hearing aids lowers the risk of decline, with some encouraging results. He also drew attention to a simpler point: a name that was never heard properly can never be remembered, and the brain of a person with unrecognised hearing loss must work harder to decode every conversation. Leila thought of all the times she had asked people to repeat themselves, and booked a hearing check for the following week, just to be sure.

Two more items on the list, Ravi said, were high blood pressure and raised cholesterol in midlife, both of which can harm the blood vessels of the brain over the years. Neither usually causes symptoms, which is why a regular check with a nurse or doctor is the only reliable way to know, and treatment is available when it is needed. Exercise helps to keep both in a healthier range, but he repeated that it is not a substitute for medical care when medical care is advised.

There is no single brain food, Ravi said firmly, whatever the labels on the supplements might claim. Patterns of eating that resemble the Mediterranean style, with plenty of vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, nuts, fish and olive oil, are linked with better brain health, although most of it is observational and cannot prove cause. The practical message, he said, was a varied diet that is good for the heart, and nobody should buy an expensive supplement for the brain without asking a doctor or pharmacist.

Water matters too, Ravi told her, because studies of volunteers show that even mild dehydration can make concentration and mood a little worse, so a glass within reach is a sensible habit. Alcohol is a different story: heavy drinking harms the brain and is listed among the risk factors for dementia, so anyone unsure how much is too much should check their own country's guidelines. Leila, who drank one glass of wine on Fridays, felt neither saintly nor alarmed.

Smoking, Ravi said, damages the heart and the small vessels of the brain, and it appears on the list of risk factors for dementia alongside many other illnesses. Mr Hughes, who had joined them on the path, said that he had given up forty years ago after a bad winter cough and a stern word from his wife, and he had never regretted a day of it. The encouraging fact, Ravi added, is that the risks fall after a person stops, whatever their age, and that free support is available in most places for anyone who wants to quit.

Ravi's favourite example was a Finnish trial called FINGER, in which more than twelve hundred older adults at risk received either health advice or a two-year programme of exercise, diet, brain training and health checks. At the end the programme group scored a little higher on thinking tests than the comparison group, a modest but encouraging difference. Later trials elsewhere have followed the same idea with varying results, he said, but the message that several small habits together may do more than any single one was hard to ignore.

Ravi wanted her to understand the difference between ordinary forgetfulness and something worth investigating. Repeating the same question within minutes, getting lost on a familiar route, struggling with tasks that used to be easy, or personality changes that others notice are reasons to see a doctor, he said. Many causes of memory trouble can be treated, among them thyroid problems, low vitamin levels, depression, poor sleep and side effects from medicines, so going early is never a waste of anybody's time.

On Monday morning Leila finally sat in Dr Amin's consulting room and described everything: the lost keys, the forgotten name, the sleepless winter and the new routine of walks, dance and strength exercises. The doctor listened without hurry, measured her blood pressure, asked a series of careful questions about her daily life and arranged some routine blood tests to look for treatable causes such as thyroid trouble. Leila left feeling not that she had been told her fears were foolish, but that somebody trained to judge them was now paying proper attention.

Dr Amin repeated what Ravi had said, but with a professional's authority: anyone with a health condition, or returning to exercise after a long gap, should talk to a doctor first and start gently. Chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness or fainting during exercise are signs to stop at once and seek medical help, and in an emergency to call the emergency number without delay. Leila, who had walked for three weeks without checking, resolved to be more careful and to rely less on luck.

Her office stood on the third floor, and until that week Leila had taken the lift every day without a thought. Now she climbed the stairs at least twice a day, a little out of breath at the top but pleased, and Ravi reminded her that short bursts of activity count towards the total just as longer sessions do. Even ten minutes of movement is better than none, he said, and the stairs were free, always open and a good deal faster than waiting.

Ravi mentioned that some small studies of interval training, in which short bursts of hard effort alternate with easy recovery, have found larger rises in BDNF than steady exercise does. Leila tried a very gentle version on the towpath, walking fast between two lamp-posts for thirty seconds and then strolling for two minutes, and she came home breathless, flushed and very pleased with herself. Moderate activity is enough for most people, he stressed, and anyone with health worries should ask a doctor before trying hard bursts.

Habits, Ravi said, are built from a cue and a routine, and the easiest way to create one is to attach the new action to something that already happens every day: after the morning tea, the trainers go on. In one well-known study volunteers took about two months on average to make a new behaviour automatic, though the range was enormous, from under three weeks to more than eight months. Leila did the sum and realised that her walks, now a month old, were only halfway to being something she did without thinking.

In the fourth week Leila caught a heavy cold and for seven days did nothing more strenuous than shuffle to the kettle, and she lay in bed convinced that she had wrecked everything. Ravi told her that rest is the right response to a proper illness, that missing a day made little difference in the habit study, and that she should return gently when she was well. A common rule of thumb, he added, is that light exercise is fine with a head cold, though not with a fever or a chest infection, and anyone unsure should ask a doctor or pharmacist.

People keep up exercise that they enjoy, Ravi said, and give up exercise that they dread, which means that enjoyment is not a luxury but a method. Leila considered her options, set the dance class and the canal walks firmly on the list, and put the idea of the treadmill, with its blank wall and its grinding noise, at the very bottom. The right activity is the one that she would still be doing in a year's time, he said, and if that turned out to be gardening, then gardening it would be.

A goal like getting fit is too vague to act on, Ravi explained, whereas a plan that says exactly when, where and how long gives the mind a trigger to follow. Studies of such if-then plans suggest that they help many people to follow through, and Leila wrote on a sticky note After breakfast on weekdays, I will walk for twenty minutes. She stuck it to the refrigerator door, where it looked rather like an entry in a ledger, which she found reassuring, since she had always been good at doing what was written down.

Ravi had one more list, and it was a practical one: comfortable shoes with a good grip, something bright to wear in poor light, a charged phone in the pocket and a word to a friend about the route. On the canal path he asked her to take extra care near the water's edge, where wet leaves can make the stones slippery, and to give way to cyclists, who tend to appear without warning from behind. It was not exciting advice, he said, but it was the kind that keeps a walking habit going for decades.

Ravi suggested that she track her progress somewhere visible, and Leila hung a calendar in the kitchen and drew a bold tick on every day that she walked. The chain of ticks grew steadily, apart from one blank week in the middle for the cold, and she discovered that the wish not to break the chain was a surprisingly strong motivator. When the second fortnight ended with an almost unbroken line of ticks, she rewarded herself with a pair of thick new walking socks, which pleased her more than a box of chocolates would have done.

By the end of the fourth week, Leila walked through the Saturday market without a shopping list and came home with every single item, including the one that she would normally have forgotten. She had not lost her keys once since the evening of the zipped pocket, and she could recall the names of everyone at the dance class. Ravi was delighted for her, but he reminded her gently that many things could explain the change, from better sleep and less stress to the simple fact that she had stopped dreading her own mistakes.

That evening Leila asked the question that she had been saving up: did her own month prove that exercise worked? Ravi shook his head with great affection and said that she was one person with no comparison group, and that hope, chance and the natural tendency of bad patches to improve might all have played a part. Her experience was real and valuable, he said, and it could suggest ideas, but only large fair trials could show what exercise does for people in general.

On their last walk but one, Ravi summed up the lesson of the month in a few plain sentences. Exercise is not a magic pill, he said, and its effects on thinking are modest, but it is one of the few things that helps the heart, the mood, the sleep, the muscles and probably the brain all at once. Sleep, learning, food, friends and a calm mind matter just as much, and the best plan is to work on all of them gently and together.

On the back of the envelope that had started the month, Ravi drew three columns and sorted everything they had learned. The first, well established, held heart health, mood, sleep, strength and balance, while the second, promising, held some benefits for attention and planning and a possible lower risk of dementia. The third, unknown, held the exact mechanisms, the best amount and the question of whether exercise can slow a disease that has begun, and Leila trusted anyone who could draw that column so clearly.

Without being asked, Joan, Marcus, Mr Hughes and Nadia decided that the walking should not end when Ravi went home, and they proposed a regular Wednesday walk along the canal at half past seven. They named themselves the Canal Walkers, a title that Mr Hughes pronounced both dignified and slightly dangerous, and Biscuit led them off with the confidence of a field marshal. Leila stood at the lock gates watching a line of coats and scarves stretch out along the towpath and realised that her private experiment had quietly become a small community.

On the last morning Ravi packed his rucksack, heavier now by a jar of Leila's lemon pickle, and she walked with him to the station through the first thin frost of the year. On the platform she held up the blue notebook like a certificate and promised to keep walking, strengthening, dancing and writing in it, and he made her promise to ring him on Sundays. As the train pulled away, he leaned out of the window to wave, and she stood watching until it had disappeared, with a lump in her throat that was entirely different from fear.

That evening, in the quiet that follows a guest's departure, Leila drew up a plan for each week and fastened it to the refrigerator door, a plan so simple that it fitted on half a sheet. It contained brisk walks on most days, strength exercises on two of them, dance on Thursday, a Spanish lesson on Tuesday, early nights, a glass of water by the bed and time with friends. Nothing on the list was heroic, she thought, and that was exactly why she expected it to last.

A few days later Dr Amin telephoned to say that the blood tests had shown nothing unusual, and that the hearing check Leila had booked was a sensible next step. She suggested a review in six months and asked Leila to come back sooner if her worries changed, or if her family noticed that she was becoming confused about familiar things. Leila put down the phone with relief and wrote the review date in her notebook, understanding that peace of mind now depended on looking after herself regularly and not on hoping to escape every worry.

On the first morning without Ravi the drizzle fell in fine grey threads, and Leila walked the canal path alone, hearing a voice in her head that explained things in her nephew's patient tone. Back at the house she hung up her wet coat and found, with only a little surprise, that her keys were hanging exactly where she had told them to hang. Then she opened the blue notebook and wrote on a clean page the sentence that seemed to sum up the whole month, which was start where you are.

On Sunday evening Ravi telephoned, and Leila told him that she had just finished a long walk beside the canal, with the sun going down in red and gold. This book has offered only general information, and it is not medical advice, so it cannot replace a conversation with a doctor who knows your own health and history. Whatever your age, he said, a little movement most days is a kind thing to do for your body and your mind, so go on, put on your shoes.
